## Basic Types — 20.17. Byte Arrays {#manual-basic-types-2017-byte-arrays}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Byte-Arrays/

Byte arrays are a specialized array type that can only contain elements of type `[UInt8]](#manual-UInt8___ofBitVec)`.
Due to this restriction, they can use a much more efficient representation, with no pointer indirections.
Like other arrays, byte arrays are represented in compiled code as [dynamic arrays]](#manual---tech-term-dynamic-arrays), and the Lean runtime specially optimizes array operations.
The operations that modify byte arrays first check the array's [reference count]](#manual-reference-counting), and if there are no other references to the array, it is modified in place.

There is no literal syntax for byte arrays.
`[List.toByteArray]](#manual-List___toByteArray)` can be used to construct an array from a list literal.

structure

```lean
[ByteArray]](#manual-ByteArray___mk) : Type



[ByteArray]](#manual-ByteArray___mk) : Type
```

`[ByteArray]](#manual-ByteArray___mk)` is like `[Array]](#manual-Array___mk) [UInt8]](#manual-UInt8___ofBitVec)`, but with an efficient run-time representation as a packed
byte buffer.

Constructor

```lean
[ByteArray.mk]](#manual-ByteArray___mk)
```

Packs an array of bytes into a `[ByteArray]](#manual-ByteArray___mk)`.

Converting between `[Array]](#manual-Array___mk)` and `[ByteArray]](#manual-ByteArray___mk)` takes linear time.

Fields

```lean
data : [Array]](#manual-Array___mk) [UInt8]](#manual-UInt8___ofBitVec)
```

The data contained in the byte array.

Converting between `[Array]](#manual-Array___mk)` and `[ByteArray]](#manual-ByteArray___mk)` takes linear time.

Appends two byte arrays using fast array primitives instead of converting them into lists and back.

In compiled code, this function replaces calls to `[ByteArray.append]](#manual-ByteArray___append)`.

def

```lean
[ByteArray.copySlice]](#manual-ByteArray___copySlice) (src : [ByteArray]](#manual-ByteArray___mk)) (srcOff : [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero)) (dest : [ByteArray]](#manual-ByteArray___mk))
  (destOff len : [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero)) (exact : [Bool]](#manual-Bool___false) := [true]](#manual-Bool___false)) : [ByteArray]](#manual-ByteArray___mk)



[ByteArray.copySlice]](#manual-ByteArray___copySlice) (src : [ByteArray]](#manual-ByteArray___mk))
  (srcOff : [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero)) (dest : [ByteArray]](#manual-ByteArray___mk))
  (destOff len : [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero))
  (exact : [Bool]](#manual-Bool___false) := [true]](#manual-Bool___false)) : [ByteArray]](#manual-ByteArray___mk)
```

Copies the slice at `[srcOff, srcOff + len)` in `src` to `[destOff, destOff + len)` in
`dest`, growing `dest` if necessary. If `exact` is `[false]](#manual-Bool___false)`, the capacity
will be doubled when grown.

#### 20.17.1.2. Size {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Basic-Types--Byte-Arrays--API-Reference--Size}

def

```lean
[ByteArray.size]](#manual-ByteArray___size) : [ByteArray]](#manual-ByteArray___mk) → [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero)



[ByteArray.size]](#manual-ByteArray___size) : [ByteArray]](#manual-ByteArray___mk) → [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero)
```

Returns the number of bytes in the byte array.

This is the number of bytes actually in the array, as distinct from its capacity, which is the
amount of memory presently allocated for the array.

def

```lean
[ByteArray.usize]](#manual-ByteArray___usize) (a : [ByteArray]](#manual-ByteArray___mk)) : [USize]](#manual-USize___ofBitVec)



[ByteArray.usize]](#manual-ByteArray___usize) (a : [ByteArray]](#manual-ByteArray___mk)) : [USize]](#manual-USize___ofBitVec)
```

Retrieves the size of the array as a platform-specific fixed-width integer.

Because `[USize]](#manual-USize___ofBitVec)` is big enough to address all memory on every platform that Lean supports,
there are in practice no `[ByteArray]](#manual-ByteArray___mk)`s that have more elements that `[USize]](#manual-USize___ofBitVec)` can count.

def

```lean
[ByteArray.isEmpty]](#manual-ByteArray___isEmpty) (s : [ByteArray]](#manual-ByteArray___mk)) : [Bool]](#manual-Bool___false)



[ByteArray.isEmpty]](#manual-ByteArray___isEmpty) (s : [ByteArray]](#manual-ByteArray___mk)) : [Bool]](#manual-Bool___false)
```

Returns `[true]](#manual-Bool___false)` when `s` contains zero bytes.

#### 20.17.1.3. Lookups {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Basic-Types--Byte-Arrays--API-Reference--Lookups}

def

```lean
[ByteArray.get]](#manual-ByteArray___get) (a : [ByteArray]](#manual-ByteArray___mk)) (i : [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero))
  (h : i [<]](#manual-LT___mk) a.[size]](#manual-ByteArray___size) := by get_elem_tactic) : [UInt8]](#manual-UInt8___ofBitVec)
```

Retrieves the byte at the indicated index. Callers must prove that the index is in bounds.

Use `uget` for a more efficient alternative or `get!` for a variant that panics if the
index is out of bounds.

def

```lean
[ByteArray.uget]](#manual-ByteArray___uget) (a : [ByteArray]](#manual-ByteArray___mk)) (i : [USize]](#manual-USize___ofBitVec))

```

Retrieves the byte at the indicated index. Callers must prove that the index is in bounds. The index
is represented by a platform-specific fixed-width integer (either 32 or 64 bits).

Because `[USize]](#manual-USize___ofBitVec)` is big enough to address all memory on every platform that Lean supports, there are
in practice no `[ByteArray]](#manual-ByteArray___mk)`s for which `uget` cannot retrieve all elements.

##### 20.17.1.4.1. UTF-8 {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Basic-Types--Byte-Arrays--API-Reference--Conversions--UTF-8}

def

```lean
[ByteArray.utf8Decode?]](#manual-ByteArray___utf8Decode___) (b : [ByteArray]](#manual-ByteArray___mk)) : [Option]](#manual-Option___none) ([Array]](#manual-Array___mk) [Char]](#manual-Char___mk))



[ByteArray.utf8Decode?]](#manual-ByteArray___utf8Decode___) (b : [ByteArray]](#manual-ByteArray___mk)) :
  [Option]](#manual-Option___none) ([Array]](#manual-Array___mk) [Char]](#manual-Char___mk))
```

Decodes a sequence of characters from their UTF-8 representation. Returns `[none]](#manual-Option___none)` if the bytes are
not a sequence of Unicode scalar values.

def

```lean
[ByteArray.utf8DecodeChar?]](#manual-ByteArray___utf8DecodeChar___) (bytes : [ByteArray]](#manual-ByteArray___mk)) (i : [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero)) : [Option]](#manual-Option___none) [Char]](#manual-Char___mk)



[ByteArray.utf8DecodeChar?]](#manual-ByteArray___utf8DecodeChar___)
  (bytes : [ByteArray]](#manual-ByteArray___mk)) (i : [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero)) :
  [Option]](#manual-Option___none) [Char]](#manual-Char___mk)
```

Decodes and returns the `[Char]](#manual-Char___mk)` whose UTF-8 encoding begins at `i` in `bytes`.

Returns `[none]](#manual-Option___none)` if `i` is not the start of a valid UTF-8 encoding of a character.

def

```lean
[ByteArray.utf8DecodeChar]](#manual-ByteArray___utf8DecodeChar) (bytes : [ByteArray]](#manual-ByteArray___mk)) (i : [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero))
  (h : (bytes.[utf8DecodeChar?]](#manual-ByteArray___utf8DecodeChar___) i).[isSome]](#manual-Option___isSome) [=]](#manual-Eq___refl) [true]](#manual-Bool___false)) : [Char]](#manual-Char___mk)



[ByteArray.utf8DecodeChar]](#manual-ByteArray___utf8DecodeChar)
  (bytes : [ByteArray]](#manual-ByteArray___mk)) (i : [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero))
  (h :
    (bytes.[utf8DecodeChar?]](#manual-ByteArray___utf8DecodeChar___) i).[isSome]](#manual-Option___isSome) [=]](#manual-Eq___refl)
      [true]](#manual-Bool___false)) :
  [Char]](#manual-Char___mk)
```

Decodes and returns the `[Char]](#manual-Char___mk)` whose UTF-8 encoding begins at `i` in `bytes`.

This function requires a proof that there is, in fact, a valid `[Char]](#manual-Char___mk)` at `i`. `utf8DecodeChar?` is
an alternative function that returns `[Option]](#manual-Option___none) [Char]](#manual-Char___mk)` instead of requiring a proof ahead of time.

#### 20.17.1.5. Modification {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Basic-Types--Byte-Arrays--API-Reference--Modification}

def

```lean
[ByteArray.push]](#manual-ByteArray___push) : [ByteArray]](#manual-ByteArray___mk) → [UInt8]](#manual-UInt8___ofBitVec) → [ByteArray]](#manual-ByteArray___mk)



[ByteArray.push]](#manual-ByteArray___push) :
  [ByteArray]](#manual-ByteArray___mk) → [UInt8]](#manual-UInt8___ofBitVec) → [ByteArray]](#manual-ByteArray___mk)
```

Adds an element to the end of an array. The resulting array's size is one greater than the input
array. If there are no other references to the array, then it is modified in-place.

This takes amortized `O(1)` time because `[ByteArray]](#manual-ByteArray___mk)` is represented by a dynamic array.

def

```lean
[ByteArray.set]](#manual-ByteArray___set) (a : [ByteArray]](#manual-ByteArray___mk)) (i : [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero)) :
  [UInt8]](#manual-UInt8___ofBitVec) → (h : [autoParam]](#manual-autoParam) [(]](#manual-LT___mk)i [<]](#manual-LT___mk) a.[size]](#manual-ByteArray___size)[)]](#manual-LT___mk) ByteArray.set._auto_1) → [ByteArray]](#manual-ByteArray___mk)



[ByteArray.set]](#manual-ByteArray___set) (a : [ByteArray]](#manual-ByteArray___mk)) (i : [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero)) :
  [UInt8]](#manual-UInt8___ofBitVec) →
    (h :
        [autoParam]](#manual-autoParam) [(]](#manual-LT___mk)i [<]](#manual-LT___mk) a.[size]](#manual-ByteArray___size)[)]](#manual-LT___mk)
          ByteArray.set._auto_1) →
      [ByteArray]](#manual-ByteArray___mk)
```

Replaces the byte at the given index.

No bounds check is performed, but the function requires a proof that the index is in bounds. This
proof can usually be omitted, and will be synthesized automatically.

The array is modified in-place if there are no other references to it.

```lean
      [ByteArray]](#manual-ByteArray___mk)



[ByteArray.uset]](#manual-ByteArray___uset) (a : [ByteArray]](#manual-ByteArray___mk))
  (i : [USize]](#manual-USize___ofBitVec)) :
  [UInt8]](#manual-UInt8___ofBitVec) →
    (h :
        [autoParam]](#manual-autoParam) [(]](#manual-LT___mk)i.[toNat]](#manual-USize___toNat) [<]](#manual-LT___mk) a.[size]](#manual-ByteArray___size)[)]](#manual-LT___mk)
          ByteArray.uset._auto_1) →
      [ByteArray]](#manual-ByteArray___mk)
```

Replaces the byte at the given index.

No bounds check is performed, but the function requires a proof that the index is in bounds. This
proof can usually be omitted, and will be synthesized automatically.

The array is modified in-place if there are no other references to it.

```lean
[ByteArray.set!]](#manual-ByteArray___set___) : [ByteArray]](#manual-ByteArray___mk) → [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero) → [UInt8]](#manual-UInt8___ofBitVec) → [ByteArray]](#manual-ByteArray___mk)

```

Replaces the byte at the given index.

The array is modified in-place if there are no other references to it.

If the index is out of bounds, the array is returned unmodified.

#### 20.17.1.6. Iteration {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Basic-Types--Byte-Arrays--API-Reference--Iteration}

def

```lean
[ByteArray.foldl.{v}]](#manual-ByteArray___foldl) {β : Type v} (f : β → [UInt8]](#manual-UInt8___ofBitVec) → β) (init : β)
  (as : [ByteArray]](#manual-ByteArray___mk)) (start : [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero) := 0) (stop : [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero) := as.[size]](#manual-ByteArray___size)) : β



[ByteArray.foldl.{v}]](#manual-ByteArray___foldl) {β : Type v}
  (f : β → [UInt8]](#manual-UInt8___ofBitVec) → β) (init : β)
  (as : [ByteArray]](#manual-ByteArray___mk)) (start : [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero) := 0)
  (stop : [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero) := as.[size]](#manual-ByteArray___size)) : β
```

A left fold on `[ByteArray]](#manual-ByteArray___mk)` that iterates over an array from low to high indices, computing a
running value.

Each element of the array is combined with the value from the prior elements using a function
`f`. The initial value `init` is the starting value before any elements have been
processed.

`[ByteArray.foldlM]](#manual-ByteArray___foldlM)` is a monadic variant of this function.

```lean
  (stop : [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero) := as.[size]](#manual-ByteArray___size)) : m β

  {m : Type v → Type w} [[Monad]](#manual-Monad___mk) m]
  (f : β → [UInt8]](#manual-UInt8___ofBitVec) → m β) (init : β)
  (as : [ByteArray]](#manual-ByteArray___mk)) (start : [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero) := 0)
  (stop : [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero) := as.[size]](#manual-ByteArray___size)) : m β
```

A monadic left fold on `[ByteArray]](#manual-ByteArray___mk)` that iterates over an array from low to high indices,
computing a running value.

Each element of the array is combined with the value from the prior elements using a monadic
function `f`. The initial value `init` is the starting value before any elements have
been processed.

def

```lean
[ByteArray.forIn.{v, w}]](#manual-ByteArray___forIn) {β : Type v} {m : Type v → Type w} [[Monad]](#manual-Monad___mk) m]
  (as : [ByteArray]](#manual-ByteArray___mk)) (b : β) (f : [UInt8]](#manual-UInt8___ofBitVec) → β → m ([ForInStep]](#manual-ForInStep___done) β)) : m β
```

#### 20.17.1.7. Iterators {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Basic-Types--Byte-Arrays--API-Reference--Iterators}

def

```lean
[ByteArray.iter]](#manual-ByteArray___iter) (arr : [ByteArray]](#manual-ByteArray___mk)) : [ByteArray.Iterator]](#manual-ByteArray___Iterator___mk)



[ByteArray.iter]](#manual-ByteArray___iter) (arr : [ByteArray]](#manual-ByteArray___mk)) :
  [ByteArray.Iterator]](#manual-ByteArray___Iterator___mk)
```

Creates an iterator at the beginning of an array.

structure

```lean
[ByteArray.Iterator]](#manual-ByteArray___Iterator___mk) : Type



[ByteArray.Iterator]](#manual-ByteArray___Iterator___mk) : Type
```

Iterator over the bytes (`[UInt8]](#manual-UInt8___ofBitVec)`) of a `[ByteArray]](#manual-ByteArray___mk)`.

Typically created by `arr.iter`, where `arr` is a `[ByteArray]](#manual-ByteArray___mk)`.

An iterator is *valid* if the position `i` is *valid* for the array `arr`, meaning `0 ≤ i ≤ arr.size`

Most operations on iterators return arbitrary values if the iterator is not valid. The functions in
the `[ByteArray.Iterator]](#manual-ByteArray___Iterator___mk)` API should rule out the creation of invalid iterators, with two exceptions:

- `Iterator.next iter` is invalid if `iter` is already at the end of the array (`iter.atEnd` is
  `[true]](#manual-Bool___false)`)
- `Iterator.forward iter n`/`Iterator.nextn iter n` is invalid if `n` is strictly greater than the
  number of remaining bytes.

Constructor

```lean
[ByteArray.Iterator.mk]](#manual-ByteArray___Iterator___mk)
```

Fields

```lean
array : [ByteArray]](#manual-ByteArray___mk)
```

The array the iterator is for.

```lean
idx : [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero)
```

The current position.

This position is not necessarily valid for the array, for instance if one keeps calling
`Iterator.next` when `Iterator.atEnd` is true. If the position is not valid, then the
current byte is `([default]](#manual-Inhabited___mk) : [UInt8]](#manual-UInt8___ofBitVec))`.

The current position.

This position is not necessarily valid for the array, for instance if one keeps calling

A byte slice contains a byte array together with the start and end indices of a region of interest.

Folds a monadic operation from right to left over the bytes in a byte slice.

An accumulator of type `β` is constructed by starting with `init` and monadically combining each
byte of the byte slice with the current accumulator value in turn, moving from the end to the
start. The monad in question may permit early termination or repetition.

Examples:

```
#eval (ByteArray.mk #[1, 2, 3]).toByteSlice.foldrM (init := 0) fun x acc =>
  some x.toNat + acc
```

## Basic Types — 20.18. Ranges {#manual-basic-types-2018-ranges}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Ranges/

A *range* represents a series of consecutive elements of some type, from a lower bound to an upper bound.
The bounds may be open, in which case the bound value is not part of the range, or closed, in which case the bound value is part of the range.
Either bound may be omitted, in which case the range extends infinitely in the corresponding direction.

Ranges have dedicated syntax that consists of a starting point, `...`, and an ending point.
The starting point may be either `*`, which denotes a range that continues infinitely downwards, or a term, which denotes a range with a specific starting value.
By default, ranges are left-closed: they contain their starting points.
A trailing `<` indicates that the range is left-open and does not contain its starting point.
The ending point may be `*`, in which case the range continues infinitely upwards, or a term, which denotes a range with a specific ending value.
By default, ranges are right-open: they do not contain their ending points.
The ending point may be prefixed with `<` to indicate that it is right-open; this is the default and does not change the meaning, but may be easier to read.
It may also be prefixed with `=` to indicate that the range is right-closed and contains its ending point.

**Example: Ranges of Natural Numbers**

The range that contains the numbers `3` through `6` can be written in a variety of ways:

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) (3...7).[toList]](#manual-Std___Rco___toList)
```

```lean
[[]](#manual-List___nil)3[,]](#manual-List___nil) 4[,]](#manual-List___nil) 5[,]](#manual-List___nil) 6[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)
```

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) (3...=6).[toList]](#manual-Std___Rcc___toList)
```

```lean
[[]](#manual-List___nil)3[,]](#manual-List___nil) 4[,]](#manual-List___nil) 5[,]](#manual-List___nil) 6[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)
```

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) (2<...=6).[toList]](#manual-Std___Roc___toList)
```

```lean
[[]](#manual-List___nil)3[,]](#manual-List___nil) 4[,]](#manual-List___nil) 5[,]](#manual-List___nil) 6[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)
```

**Example: Finite and Infinite Ranges**

This range cannot be converted to a list, because it is infinite:

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) (3...*).[toList]](#manual-Std___Rci___toList)
```

Finiteness of a left-closed, right-unbounded range is indicated by the presence of an instance of `[Std.Rxi.IsAlwaysFinite]](#manual-Std___Rxi___IsAlwaysFinite___mk)`, which does not exist for `[Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero)`.
`[Std.Rco]](#manual-Std___Rco___mk)` is the type of these ranges, and the name `[Std.Rxi.IsAlwaysFinite]](#manual-Std___Rxi___IsAlwaysFinite___mk)` indicates that it determines finiteness for all right-unbounded ranges.

```lean
failed to synthesize instance of type class
  [Std.Rxi.IsAlwaysFinite]](#manual-Std___Rxi___IsAlwaysFinite___mk) [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero)

Hint: Type class instance resolution failures can be inspected with the `set_option trace.Meta.synthInstance true` command.
```

Attempting to enumerate the negative integers leads to a similar error, this time because there is no way to determine the least element:

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) (*...(0 : [Int]](#manual-Int___ofNat))).[toList]](#manual-Std___Rio___toList)
```

```lean
failed to synthesize instance of type class
  [Std.PRange.Least?]](#manual-Std___PRange___Least______mk) [Int]](#manual-Int___ofNat)

Hint: Type class instance resolution failures can be inspected with the `set_option trace.Meta.synthInstance true` command.
```

Unbounded ranges in finite types indicate that the range extends to the greatest element of the type.
Because `[UInt8]](#manual-UInt8___ofBitVec)` has 256 elements, this range contains 253 elements:

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) ((3 : [UInt8]](#manual-UInt8___ofBitVec))...*).[toArray]](#manual-Std___Rci___toArray).[size]](#manual-Array___size)
```

```lean
253
```

syntaxRange Syntax

This range is left-closed, right-open, and indicates `[Std.Rco]](#manual-Std___Rco___mk)`:

```lean
term ::= ...
    | term...term
```

This range is left-closed, right-open, and indicates `[Std.Rco]](#manual-Std___Rco___mk)`:

```lean
term ::= ...
    | term...<term
```

This range is left-closed, right-closed, and indicates `[Std.Rcc]](#manual-Std___Rcc___mk)`:

```lean
term ::= ...
    | term...=term
```

This range is left-closed, right-infinite, and indicates `[Std.Rci]](#manual-Std___Rci___mk)`:

```lean
term ::= ...
    | term...*
```

This range is left-open, right-open, and indicates `[Std.Roo]](#manual-Std___Roo___mk)`:

```lean
term ::= ...
    | term<...term
```

This range is left-open, right-open, and indicates `[Std.Roo]](#manual-Std___Roo___mk)`:

```lean
term ::= ...
    | term<...<term
```

This range is left-open, right-closed, and indicates `[Std.Roc]](#manual-Std___Roc___mk)`:

```lean
term ::= ...
    | term<...=term
```

This range is left-open, right-infinite, and indicates `[Std.Roi]](#manual-Std___Roi___mk)`:

```lean
term ::= ...
    | term<...*
```

This range is left-infinite, right-open, and indicates `[Std.Rio]](#manual-Std___Rio___mk)`:

```lean
term ::= ...
    | *...term
```

This range is left-infinite, right-open, and indicates `[Std.Ric]](#manual-Std___Ric___mk)`:

```lean
term ::= ...
    | *...<term
```

This range is left-infinite, right-closed, and indicates `[Std.Ric]](#manual-Std___Ric___mk)`:

```lean
term ::= ...
    | *...=term
```

This range is infinite on both sides, and indicates `[Std.Rii]](#manual-Std___Rii___mk)`:

```lean
term ::= ...
    | *...*
```

### 20.18.1. Range Types {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Basic-Types--Ranges--Range-Types}

structure

```lean
[Std.Rco.{u}]](#manual-Std___Rco___mk) (α : Type u) : Type u



[Std.Rco.{u}]](#manual-Std___Rco___mk) (α : Type u) : Type u
```

A range of elements of `α` with a closed lower bound and an open upper bound.

`a...b` or `a...<b` is the range of all values greater than or equal to `a : α` and
less than `b : α`. This is notation for `Rco.mk a b`.

Constructor

```lean
[Std.Rco.mk]](#manual-Std___Rco___mk).{u}
```

Fields

```lean
lower : α
```

The lower bound of the range. `lower` is included in the range.

```lean
upper : α
```

The upper bound of the range. `upper` is not included in the range.

def

```lean
[Std.Rco.iter.{u_1}]](#manual-Std___Rco___iter) {α : Type u_1} (r : [Std.Rco]](#manual-Std___Rco___mk) α) : [Std.Iter](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Iterators/Iterator-Definitions/#Std___Iter___mk) α



[Std.Rco.iter.{u_1}]](#manual-Std___Rco___iter) {α : Type u_1}
```

This function exists for completeness and always returns false:
The closed lower bound is contained in the range, so
left-closed right-unbounded ranges are never empty.

### 20.18.2. Range-Related Type Classes {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Basic-Types--Ranges--Range-Related-Type-Classes}

type class

```lean
[Std.PRange.UpwardEnumerable.{u}]](#manual-Std___PRange___UpwardEnumerable___mk) (α : Type u) : Type u



[Std.PRange.UpwardEnumerable.{u}]](#manual-Std___PRange___UpwardEnumerable___mk)
  (α : Type u) : Type u
```

This typeclass provides the function `succ? : α → [Option]](#manual-Option___none) α` that computes the successor of
elements of `α`, or none if no successor exists.
It also provides the function `succMany?`, which computes `n`-th successors.

`succ?` is expected to be acyclic: No element is its own transitive successor.
If `α` is ordered, then every element larger than `a : α` should be a transitive successor of `a`.
These properties and the compatibility of `succ?` with `succMany?` are encoded in the typeclasses
`LawfulUpwardEnumerable`, `LawfulUpwardEnumerableLE` and `LawfulUpwardEnumerableLT`.

Instance Constructor

```lean
[Std.PRange.UpwardEnumerable.mk]](#manual-Std___PRange___UpwardEnumerable___mk).{u}
```

Methods

```lean
succ? : α → [Option]](#manual-Option___none) α
```

Maps elements of `α` to their successor, or none if no successor exists.

```lean
succMany? : [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero) → α → [Option]](#manual-Option___none) α
```

Maps elements of `α` to their `n`-th successor, or none if no successor exists.
This should semantically behave like repeatedly applying `succ?`, but it might be more efficient.

`LawfulUpwardEnumerable` ensures the compatibility with `succ?`.

If no other implementation is provided in `UpwardEnumerable` instance, `succMany?` repeatedly
applies `succ?`.

def

```lean
[Std.PRange.UpwardEnumerable.LE.{u}]](#manual-Std___PRange___UpwardEnumerable___LE) {α : Type u}
  [[Std.PRange.UpwardEnumerable]](#manual-Std___PRange___UpwardEnumerable___mk) α] (a b : α) : Prop



[Std.PRange.UpwardEnumerable.LE.{u}]](#manual-Std___PRange___UpwardEnumerable___LE)
  {α : Type u}
  [[Std.PRange.UpwardEnumerable]](#manual-Std___PRange___UpwardEnumerable___mk) α]
  (a b : α) : Prop
```

According to `UpwardEnumerable.LE`, `a` is less than or equal to `b` if `b` is `a` or a transitive
successor of `a`.

def

```lean
[Std.PRange.UpwardEnumerable.LT.{u}]](#manual-Std___PRange___UpwardEnumerable___LT) {α : Type u}
```

According to `UpwardEnumerable.LT`, `a` is less than `b` if `b` is a proper transitive successor of
`a`. 'Proper' means that `b` is the `n`-th successor of `a`, where `n > 0`.

Given `LawfulUpwardEnumerable α`, no element of `α` is less than itself.


The `n + 1`-th successor of `a` is the successor of the `n`-th successor, given that said
successors actually exist.

The typeclass `Least? α` optionally provides a smallest element of `α`, `least? : [Option]](#manual-Option___none) α`.

The main use case of this typeclass is to use it in combination with `UpwardEnumerable` to
obtain a (possibly infinite) ascending enumeration of all elements of `α`.

```lean
[Std.PRange.Least?.mk]](#manual-Std___PRange___Least______mk).{u}
```


Returns the smallest element of `α`, or none if `α` is empty.

Only empty types are allowed to define `least? := none`. If `α` is ordered and nonempty, then
the value of `least?` should be the smallest element according to the order on `α`.


### 20.18.3. Implementing Ranges {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Basic-Types--Ranges--Implementing-Ranges}

The built-in range types may be used with any type, but their usefulness depends on the presence of certain type class instances.
Generally speaking, ranges are either checked for membership, enumerated or iterated over.
To check whether an value is contained in a range, `[DecidableLT]](#manual-DecidableLT)` and `[DecidableLE]](#manual-DecidableLE)` instances are used to compare the value to the range's respective open and closed endpoints.
To get an iterator for a range, instances of `[Std.PRange.UpwardEnumerable]](#manual-Std___PRange___UpwardEnumerable___mk)` and `[Std.PRange.LawfulUpwardEnumerable]](#manual-Std___PRange___LawfulUpwardEnumerable___mk)` are all that's needed.
To iterate directly over it in a `for` loop, `Std.PRange.LawfulUpwardEnumerableLE` and `Std.PRange.LawfulUpwardEnumerableLT` are required as well.
To enumerate a range (e.g. by calling `[toList]](#manual-Std___Rco___toList)`), it must be proven finite.
This is done by supplying instances of `[Std.Rxi.IsAlwaysFinite]](#manual-Std___Rxi___IsAlwaysFinite___mk)`, `[Std.Rxc.IsAlwaysFinite]](#manual-Std___Rxc___IsAlwaysFinite___mk)`, or `Std.Rxo.IsAlwaysFinite`.

**Example: Implementing Ranges**

The enumeration type `[Day]](#manual-Day-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_)` represents the days of the week:

```lean
inductive Day where
| mo | tu | we | th | fr | sa | su
[deriving]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___optDeriving-next) [Repr]](#manual-Repr___mk)
```

While it's already possible to use this type in ranges, they're not particularly useful.
There's no membership instance:

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [Day.we]](#manual-Day___we-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_) ∈ ([Day.mo]](#manual-Day___mo-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_)...=[Day.fr]](#manual-Day___fr-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_))
```

```lean
failed to synthesize instance of type class
  Membership [Day]](#manual-Day-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_) ([Std.Rcc]](#manual-Std___Rcc___mk) [Day]](#manual-Day-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_))

Hint: Type class instance resolution failures can be inspected with the `set_option trace.Meta.synthInstance true` command.
```

Ranges can't be iterated over:

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) show [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) [Unit]](#manual-Unit) from
for d in [Day.mo]](#manual-Day___mo-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_)...=[Day.fr]](#manual-Day___fr-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_) do
IO.println s!"It's {repr d}"
```

```lean
failed to synthesize instance of type class
  [ForIn]](#manual-ForIn___mk) [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) ([Std.Rcc]](#manual-Std___Rcc___mk) [Day]](#manual-Day-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_)) ?α

Hint: Type class instance resolution failures can be inspected with the `set_option trace.Meta.synthInstance true` command.
```

Nor can they be enumerated, even though the type is finite:

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) ([Day.sa]](#manual-Day___sa-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_)...*).[toList]](#manual-Std___Rci___toList)
```

```lean
failed to synthesize instance of type class
  [Std.PRange.UpwardEnumerable]](#manual-Std___PRange___UpwardEnumerable___mk) [Day]](#manual-Day-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_)

Hint: Type class instance resolution failures can be inspected with the `set_option trace.Meta.synthInstance true` command.
```

Membership tests require `[DecidableLT]](#manual-DecidableLT)` and `[DecidableLE]](#manual-DecidableLE)` instances.
An easy way to get these is to number each day, and compare the numbers:

```lean
def Day.toNat : [Day]](#manual-Day-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_) → [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero)
| [mo]](#manual-Day___mo-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_) => 0
| [tu]](#manual-Day___tu-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_) => 1
| [we]](#manual-Day___we-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_) => 2
| [th]](#manual-Day___th-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_) => 3
| [fr]](#manual-Day___fr-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_) => 4
| [sa]](#manual-Day___sa-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_) => 5
| [su]](#manual-Day___su-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_) => 6
instance : [LT]](#manual-LT___mk) [Day]](#manual-Day-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_) where
[lt]](#manual-LT___mk) d1 d2 := d1.[toNat]](#manual-Day___toNat-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_) < d2.[toNat]](#manual-Day___toNat-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_)
instance : [LE]](#manual-LE___mk) [Day]](#manual-Day-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_) where
[le]](#manual-LE___mk) d1 d2 := d1.[toNat]](#manual-Day___toNat-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_) ≤ d2.[toNat]](#manual-Day___toNat-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_)
instance : [DecidableLT]](#manual-DecidableLT) [Day]](#manual-Day-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_) :=
fun d1 d2 => inferInstanceAs ([Decidable]](#manual-Decidable___isFalse) (d1.[toNat]](#manual-Day___toNat-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_) < d2.[toNat]](#manual-Day___toNat-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_)))
instance : [DecidableLE]](#manual-DecidableLE) [Day]](#manual-Day-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_) :=
fun d1 d2 => inferInstanceAs ([Decidable]](#manual-Decidable___isFalse) (d1.[toNat]](#manual-Day___toNat-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_) ≤ d2.[toNat]](#manual-Day___toNat-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_)))
```

With these instances available, membership tests work as expected:

```lean
def Day.isWeekday (d : [Day]](#manual-Day-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_)) : [Bool]](#manual-Bool___false) := d ∈ [Day.mo]](#manual-Day___mo-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_)...[Day.sa]](#manual-Day___sa-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_)
```

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [Day.th]](#manual-Day___th-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_).[isWeekday]](#manual-Day___isWeekday-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_)
```

```lean
[true]](#manual-Bool___false)
```

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [Day.sa]](#manual-Day___sa-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_).[isWeekday]](#manual-Day___isWeekday-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_)
```

```lean
[false]](#manual-Bool___false)
```

Iteration and enumeration are both variants on repeatedly applying a successor function until either the upper bound of the range or the largest element of the type is reached.
This successor function is `[Std.PRange.UpwardEnumerable.succ?]](#manual-Std___PRange___UpwardEnumerable___mk)`.
It's also convenient to have a definition of the function in `[Day]](#manual-Day-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_)`'s namespace for use with generalized field notation:

```lean
def Day.succ? : [Day]](#manual-Day-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_) → [Option]](#manual-Option___none) [Day]](#manual-Day-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_)
| [mo]](#manual-Day___mo-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_) => [some]](#manual-Option___none) [tu]](#manual-Day___tu-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_)
| [tu]](#manual-Day___tu-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_) => [some]](#manual-Option___none) [we]](#manual-Day___we-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_)
| [we]](#manual-Day___we-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_) => [some]](#manual-Option___none) [th]](#manual-Day___th-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_)
| [th]](#manual-Day___th-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_) => [some]](#manual-Option___none) [fr]](#manual-Day___fr-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_)
| [fr]](#manual-Day___fr-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_) => [some]](#manual-Option___none) [sa]](#manual-Day___sa-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_)
| [sa]](#manual-Day___sa-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_) => [some]](#manual-Option___none) [su]](#manual-Day___su-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_)
| [su]](#manual-Day___su-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_) => [none]](#manual-Option___none)
instance : [Std.PRange.UpwardEnumerable]](#manual-Std___PRange___UpwardEnumerable___mk) [Day]](#manual-Day-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_) where
[succ?]](#manual-Std___PRange___UpwardEnumerable___mk) := [Day.succ?]](#manual-Day___succ___-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_)
```

Iteration also requires a proof that the implementation of `[succ?]](#manual-Std___PRange___UpwardEnumerable___mk)` is sensible.
Its properties are expressed in terms of `[Std.PRange.UpwardEnumerable.succMany?]](#manual-Std___PRange___UpwardEnumerable___mk)`, which iterates the application of `[succ?]](#manual-Std___PRange___UpwardEnumerable___mk)` a certain number of times and has a default implementation in terms of `[Nat.repeat]](#manual-Nat___repeat)` and `[succ?]](#manual-Std___PRange___UpwardEnumerable___mk)`.
In particular, an instance of `[LawfulUpwardEnumerable]](#manual-Std___PRange___LawfulUpwardEnumerable___mk)` requires proofs that `[Std.PRange.UpwardEnumerable.succMany?]](#manual-Std___PRange___UpwardEnumerable___mk)` corresponds to the default implementation along with a proof that repeatedly applying the successor never yields the same element again.

The first step is to write two helper lemmas for the two proofs about `[succMany?]](#manual-Std___PRange___UpwardEnumerable___mk)`.
While they could be written inline in the instance declaration, it's convenient for them to have the `[@[]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)simp[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Attributes/#Lean___Parser___Term___attributes-next)` attribute.

```lean
@[simp]
theorem Day.succMany?_zero (d : [Day]](#manual-Day-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_)) :
[Std.PRange.succMany?]](#manual-Std___PRange___UpwardEnumerable___mk) 0 d = [some]](#manual-Option___none) d := byd:[Day]](#manual-Day-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_)⊢ [Std.PRange.succMany?]](#manual-Std___PRange___UpwardEnumerable___mk) 0 d [=]](#manual-Eq___refl) [some]](#manual-Option___none) d
[simp]](#manual-simp) [[Std.PRange.succMany?]](#manual-Std___PRange___UpwardEnumerable___mk), [Nat.repeat]](#manual-Nat___repeat)]All goals completed! 🐙
@[simp]
theorem Day.succMany?_add_one (n : [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero)) (d : [Day]](#manual-Day-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_)) :
[Std.PRange.succMany?]](#manual-Std___PRange___UpwardEnumerable___mk) (n + 1) d =
([Std.PRange.succMany?]](#manual-Std___PRange___UpwardEnumerable___mk) n d).[bind]](#manual-Option___bind) [Std.PRange.succ?]](#manual-Std___PRange___UpwardEnumerable___mk) := byn:[Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero)d:[Day]](#manual-Day-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_)⊢ [Std.PRange.succMany?]](#manual-Std___PRange___UpwardEnumerable___mk) [(]](#manual-HAdd___mk)n [+]](#manual-HAdd___mk) 1[)]](#manual-HAdd___mk) d [=]](#manual-Eq___refl) ([Std.PRange.succMany?]](#manual-Std___PRange___UpwardEnumerable___mk) n d).[bind]](#manual-Option___bind) [Std.PRange.succ?]](#manual-Std___PRange___UpwardEnumerable___mk)
[simp]](#manual-simp) [[Std.PRange.succMany?]](#manual-Std___PRange___UpwardEnumerable___mk), [Nat.repeat]](#manual-Nat___repeat), [Std.PRange.succ?]](#manual-Std___PRange___UpwardEnumerable___mk)]All goals completed! 🐙
```

Adding a `[Std.PRange.Least?]](#manual-Std___PRange___Least______mk)` instance allows enumeration of left-unbounded ranges:

```lean
instance : [Std.PRange.Least?]](#manual-Std___PRange___Least______mk) [Day]](#manual-Day-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_) where
[least?]](#manual-Std___PRange___Least______mk) := [some]](#manual-Option___none) [.mo]](#manual-Day___mo-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_)
def allWeekdays' : [List]](#manual-List___nil) [Day]](#manual-Day-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_) := (*...[Day.sa]](#manual-Day___sa-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_)).[toList]](#manual-Std___Rio___toList)
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [allWeekdays']](#manual-allWeekdays___-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_)
```

```lean
[Day.mo, Day.tu, Day.we, Day.th, Day.fr]
```

It's also possible to create an iterator that can be enumerated, but it can't yet be used with `for`:

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) ([Day.we]](#manual-Day___we-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_)...[Day.fr]](#manual-Day___fr-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_)).[iter]](#manual-Std___Rco___iter).[toList](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Iterators/Consuming-Iterators/#Std___Iter___toList)
```

```lean
[Day.we, Day.th]
```

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) show [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) [Unit]](#manual-Unit) from [do]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do)
for d in ([Day.mo]](#manual-Day___mo-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_)...[Day.th]](#manual-Day___th-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_)).[iter]](#manual-Std___Rco___iter) do
IO.println s!"It's {repr d}."
```

The last step to enable iteration, thus making ranges of days fully-featured, is to prove that the less-than and less-than-or-equal-to relations on `[Day]](#manual-Day-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_)` correspond to the notions of inequality that are derived from iterating the successor function.
This is captured in the classes `Std.PRange.LawfulUpwardEnumerableLT` and `Std.PRange.LawfulUpwardEnumerableLE`, which require that the two notions are logically equivalent:

It is now possible to iterate over ranges of days:

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) show [IO](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/IO/Logical-Model/#IO) [Unit]](#manual-Unit) from [do]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___do)
for x in ([Day.mo]](#manual-Day___mo-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_)...[Day.th]](#manual-Day___th-_LPAR_in-Implementing-Ranges_RPAR_)).[iter]](#manual-Std___Rco___iter) do
[IO.println](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/IO/Console-Output/#IO___println) s!"It's {[repr]](#manual-repr-next) x}"
```

```lean
It's Day.mo
It's Day.tu
It's Day.we
```

### 20.18.4. Ranges and Slices {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Basic-Types--Ranges--Ranges-and-Slices}

Range syntax can be used with data structures that support slicing to select a slice of the structure.

**Example: Slicing Lists**

Lists may be sliced with any of the interval types:

```lean
def groceries :=
["apples", "bananas", "coffee", "dates", "endive", "fennel"]
```

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [groceries]](#manual-groceries-_LPAR_in-Slicing-Lists_RPAR_)[1...4] |>.toList
```

```lean
[[]](#manual-List___nil)"bananas"[,]](#manual-List___nil) "coffee"[,]](#manual-List___nil) "dates"[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)
```

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [groceries]](#manual-groceries-_LPAR_in-Slicing-Lists_RPAR_)[1...=4] |>.toList
```

```lean
[[]](#manual-List___nil)"bananas"[,]](#manual-List___nil) "coffee"[,]](#manual-List___nil) "dates"[,]](#manual-List___nil) "endive"[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)
```

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [groceries]](#manual-groceries-_LPAR_in-Slicing-Lists_RPAR_)[1...*] |>.toList
```

```lean
[[]](#manual-List___nil)"bananas"[,]](#manual-List___nil) "coffee"[,]](#manual-List___nil) "dates"[,]](#manual-List___nil) "endive"[,]](#manual-List___nil) "fennel"[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)
```

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [groceries]](#manual-groceries-_LPAR_in-Slicing-Lists_RPAR_)[1<...4] |>.toList
```

```lean
[[]](#manual-List___nil)"coffee"[,]](#manual-List___nil) "dates"[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)
```

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [groceries]](#manual-groceries-_LPAR_in-Slicing-Lists_RPAR_)[1<...=4] |>.toList
```

```lean
[[]](#manual-List___nil)"coffee"[,]](#manual-List___nil) "dates"[,]](#manual-List___nil) "endive"[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)
```

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [groceries]](#manual-groceries-_LPAR_in-Slicing-Lists_RPAR_)[*...=4] |>.toList
```

```lean
[[]](#manual-List___nil)"apples"[,]](#manual-List___nil) "bananas"[,]](#manual-List___nil) "coffee"[,]](#manual-List___nil) "dates"[,]](#manual-List___nil) "endive"[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)
```

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [groceries]](#manual-groceries-_LPAR_in-Slicing-Lists_RPAR_)[*...4] |>.toList
```

```lean
[[]](#manual-List___nil)"apples"[,]](#manual-List___nil) "bananas"[,]](#manual-List___nil) "coffee"[,]](#manual-List___nil) "dates"[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)
```

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [groceries]](#manual-groceries-_LPAR_in-Slicing-Lists_RPAR_)[*...*] |>.toList
```

```lean
[[]](#manual-List___nil)"apples"[,]](#manual-List___nil) "bananas"[,]](#manual-List___nil) "coffee"[,]](#manual-List___nil) "dates"[,]](#manual-List___nil) "endive"[,]](#manual-List___nil) "fennel"[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)
```

**Example: Custom Slices**

A `[Triple]](#manual-Triple-_LPAR_in-Custom-Slices_RPAR_)` contains three values of the same type:

```lean
structure Triple (α : Type u) where
fst : α
snd : α
thd : α
[deriving]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___optDeriving-next) [Repr]](#manual-Repr___mk)
```

Positions in a triple may be any of the fields, or just after `[thd]](#manual-Triple___thd-_LPAR_in-Custom-Slices_RPAR_)`:

```lean
inductive TriplePos where
| fst | snd | thd | done
[deriving]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___optDeriving-next) [Repr]](#manual-Repr___mk)
```

A slice of a triple consists of a triple, a starting position, and a stopping position.
The starting position is inclusive, and the stopping position exclusive:

```lean
structure TripleSlice (α : Type u) where
triple : [Triple]](#manual-Triple-_LPAR_in-Custom-Slices_RPAR_) α
start : [TriplePos]](#manual-TriplePos-_LPAR_in-Custom-Slices_RPAR_)
stop : [TriplePos]](#manual-TriplePos-_LPAR_in-Custom-Slices_RPAR_)
[deriving]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___optDeriving-next) [Repr]](#manual-Repr___mk)
```

Ranges of `[TriplePos]](#manual-TriplePos-_LPAR_in-Custom-Slices_RPAR_)` can be used to select a slice from a triple by implementing instances of each supported range type's `[Sliceable]](#manual-Std___Rco___Sliceable___mk)` class.
For example, `[Std.Rco.Sliceable]](#manual-Std___Rco___Sliceable___mk)` allows left-closed, right-open ranges to be used to slice `[Triple]](#manual-Triple-_LPAR_in-Custom-Slices_RPAR_)`s:

```lean
instance : [Std.Rco.Sliceable]](#manual-Std___Rco___Sliceable___mk) ([Triple]](#manual-Triple-_LPAR_in-Custom-Slices_RPAR_) α) [TriplePos]](#manual-TriplePos-_LPAR_in-Custom-Slices_RPAR_) ([TripleSlice]](#manual-TripleSlice-_LPAR_in-Custom-Slices_RPAR_) α) where
[mkSlice]](#manual-Std___Rco___Sliceable___mk) triple range :=
{ [triple]](#manual-TripleSlice___triple-_LPAR_in-Custom-Slices_RPAR_), [start]](#manual-TripleSlice___start-_LPAR_in-Custom-Slices_RPAR_) := range.[lower]](#manual-Std___Rco___mk), [stop]](#manual-TripleSlice___stop-_LPAR_in-Custom-Slices_RPAR_) := range.[upper]](#manual-Std___Rco___mk) }
```

```lean
def abc : [Triple]](#manual-Triple-_LPAR_in-Custom-Slices_RPAR_) [Char]](#manual-Char___mk) := ⟨'a', 'b', 'c'⟩
[open]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___open) TriplePos [in]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___in)
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [abc]](#manual-abc-_LPAR_in-Custom-Slices_RPAR_)[[snd]](#manual-TriplePos___snd-_LPAR_in-Custom-Slices_RPAR_)...[thd]](#manual-TriplePos___thd-_LPAR_in-Custom-Slices_RPAR_)]
```

```lean
{ triple := { fst := 'a', snd := 'b', thd := 'c' }, start := TriplePos.snd, stop := TriplePos.thd }
```

Infinite ranges have only a lower bound:

```lean
instance : [Std.Rci.Sliceable]](#manual-Std___Rci___Sliceable___mk) ([Triple]](#manual-Triple-_LPAR_in-Custom-Slices_RPAR_) α) [TriplePos]](#manual-TriplePos-_LPAR_in-Custom-Slices_RPAR_) ([TripleSlice]](#manual-TripleSlice-_LPAR_in-Custom-Slices_RPAR_) α) where
[mkSlice]](#manual-Std___Rci___Sliceable___mk) triple range :=
{ [triple]](#manual-TripleSlice___triple-_LPAR_in-Custom-Slices_RPAR_), [start]](#manual-TripleSlice___start-_LPAR_in-Custom-Slices_RPAR_) := range.[lower]](#manual-Std___Rci___mk), [stop]](#manual-TripleSlice___stop-_LPAR_in-Custom-Slices_RPAR_) := [.done]](#manual-TriplePos___done-_LPAR_in-Custom-Slices_RPAR_) }
[open]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___open) TriplePos [in]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___in)
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [abc]](#manual-abc-_LPAR_in-Custom-Slices_RPAR_)[[snd]](#manual-TriplePos___snd-_LPAR_in-Custom-Slices_RPAR_)...*]
```

```lean
{ triple := { fst := 'a', snd := 'b', thd := 'c' }, start := TriplePos.snd, stop := TriplePos.done }
```

type class

```lean
[Std.Rco.Sliceable.{u, v, w}]](#manual-Std___Rco___Sliceable___mk) (α : Type u) (β : [outParam]](#manual-outParam) (Type v))
  (γ : [outParam]](#manual-outParam) (Type w)) : Type (max (max u v) w)



[Std.Rco.Sliceable.{u, v, w}]](#manual-Std___Rco___Sliceable___mk) (α : Type u)
  (β : [outParam]](#manual-outParam) (Type v))
  (γ : [outParam]](#manual-outParam) (Type w)) :
  Type (max (max u v) w)
```

This typeclass indicates how to obtain slices of elements of `α` over ranges in the index type
`β`, the ranges being left-closed right-open.

The type of the resulting slices is `γ`.

Instance Constructor

```lean
[Std.Rco.Sliceable.mk]](#manual-Std___Rco___Sliceable___mk).{u, v, w}
```

Methods

```lean
mkSlice : α → [Std.Rco]](#manual-Std___Rco___mk) β → γ
```

Slices `carrier` from `range.lower` (inclusive) to `range.upper` (exclusive).

type class

```lean
[Std.Rcc.Sliceable.{u, v, w}]](#manual-Std___Rcc___Sliceable___mk) (α : Type u) (β : [outParam]](#manual-outParam) (Type v))
  (γ : [outParam]](#manual-outParam) (Type w)) : Type (max (max u v) w)



[Std.Rcc.Sliceable.{u, v, w}]](#manual-Std___Rcc___Sliceable___mk) (α : Type u)
  (β : [outParam]](#manual-outParam) (Type v))
  (γ : [outParam]](#manual-outParam) (Type w)) :
  Type (max (max u v) w)
```

This typeclass indicates how to obtain slices of elements of `α` over ranges in the index type
`β`, the ranges being closed.

The type of the resulting slices is `γ`.

Instance Constructor

```lean
[Std.Rcc.Sliceable.mk]](#manual-Std___Rcc___Sliceable___mk).{u, v, w}
```

## Basic Types — 20.19. Maps and Sets {#manual-basic-types-2019-maps-and-sets}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Maps-and-Sets/

A *map* is a data structure that associates keys with values.
They are also referred to as *dictionaries*, *associative arrays*, or simply as hash tables.

In Lean, maps may have the following properties:

Representation
:   The in-memory representation of a map may be either a tree or a hash table.
    Tree-based representations are better when the [reference]](#manual-reference-counting) to the data structure is shared, because hash tables are based on [arrays]](#manual-Array).
    Arrays are copied in full on modification when the reference is not unique, while only the path from the root of the tree to the modified nodes must be copied on modification of a tree.
    Hash tables, on the other hand, can be more efficient when references are not shared, because non-shared arrays can be modified in constant time.
    Furthermore, tree-based maps store data in order and thus support ordered traversals of the data.

Extensionality
:   Maps can be viewed as partial functions from keys to values.
    *Extensional maps* are maps for which propositional equality matches this interpretation.
    This can be convenient for reasoning, but it also rules out some useful operations that would be able to distinguish between them.
    In general, extensional maps should be used only when needed for verification.

Dependent or Not
:   A *dependent map* is one in which the type of each value is determined by its corresponding key, rather than being constant.
    Dependent maps have more expressive power, but are also more difficult to use.
    They impose more requirements on their users.
    For example, many operations on `[DHashMap]](#manual-Std___DHashMap)` require `[LawfulBEq]](#manual-LawfulBEq___mk)` instances rather than `[BEq]](#manual-BEq___mk)`.

| Map | Representation | Extensional? | Dependent? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `[TreeMap]](#manual-Std___TreeMap)` | Tree | No | No |
| `[DTreeMap]](#manual-Std___DTreeMap)` | Tree | No | Yes |
| `[HashMap]](#manual-Std___HashMap)` | Hash Table | No | No |
| `[DHashMap]](#manual-Std___DHashMap)` | Hash Table | No | Yes |
| `[ExtHashMap]](#manual-Std___ExtHashMap)` | Hash Table | Yes | No |
| `[ExtDHashMap]](#manual-Std___ExtDHashMap)` | Hash Table | Yes | Yes |

A map can always be used as a set by setting its type of values to `[Unit]](#manual-Unit)`.
The following set types are provided:

- `[Std.HashSet]](#manual-Std___HashSet___mk)` is a set based on hash tables. Its performance characteristics are like those of `[Std.HashMap]](#manual-Std___HashMap)`: it is based on arrays and can be efficiently updated, but only when not shared.
- `[Std.TreeSet]](#manual-Std___TreeSet)` is a set based on balanced trees. Its performance characteristics are like those of `[Std.TreeMap]](#manual-Std___TreeMap)`.
- `[Std.ExtHashSet]](#manual-Std___ExtHashSet___mk)` is an extensional hash set type that matches the mathematical notion of finite sets: two sets are equal if they contain the same elements.

### 20.19.1. Library Design {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Basic-Types--Maps-and-Sets--Library-Design}

All the basic operations on maps and sets are fully verified.
They are proven correct with respect to simpler models implemented with lists.
At the same time, maps and sets have predictable performance.

Some types include additional operations that are not yet fully verified.
These operations are useful, and not all programs need full verification.
Examples include `[HashMap.partition]](#manual-Std___HashMap___partition)` and `[TreeMap.filterMap]](#manual-Std___TreeMap___filterMap)`.

#### 20.19.1.1. Fused Operations {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Basic-Types--Maps-and-Sets--Library-Design--Fused-Operations}

It is common to modify a table based on its pre-existing contents.
To avoid having to traverse a data structure twice, many query/modification pairs are provided in “fused” variants that perform a query while modifying a map or set.
In some cases, the result of the query affects the modification.

For example, `[Std.HashMap]](#manual-Std___HashMap)` provides `[containsThenInsert]](#manual-Std___HashMap___containsThenInsert)`, which inserts a key-value pair into a map while signalling whether it was previously found, and `[containsThenInsertIfNew]](#manual-Std___HashMap___containsThenInsertIfNew)`, which inserts the new mapping only if it was not previously present.
The `[alter]](#manual-Std___HashMap___alter)` function modifies the value for a given key without having to search for the key multiple times; the alternation is performed by a function in which missing values are represented by `[none]](#manual-Option___none)`.

#### 20.19.1.2. Raw Data and Invariants {#manual-raw-data}

Both hash-based and tree-based maps rely on certain internal well-formedness invariants, such as that trees are balanced and ordered.
In Lean's standard library, these data structures are represented as a pair of the underlying data with a proof that it is well formed.
This fact is mostly an internal implementation detail; however, it is relevant to users in one situation: this representation prevents them from being used in [nested inductive types]](#manual---tech-term-Nested-inductive-types).

To enable their use in nested inductive types, the standard library provides “raw” variants of each container along with separate “unbundled” versions of their invariants.
These use the following naming convention:

- `T.Raw` is the version of type `T` without its invariants. For example, `[Std.HashMap.Raw]](#manual-Std___HashMap___Raw___mk)` is a version of `[Std.HashMap]](#manual-Std___HashMap)` without the embedded proofs.
- `T.Raw.WF` is the corresponding well-formedness predicate. For example, `[Std.HashMap.Raw.WF]](#manual-Std___HashMap___Raw___WF___mk)` asserts that a `[Std.HashMap.Raw]](#manual-Std___HashMap___Raw___mk)` is well-formed.
- Each operation on `T`, called `T.f`, has a corresponding operation on `T.Raw` called `T.Raw.f`. For example, `Std.HashMap.Raw.insert` is the version of `[Std.HashMap.insert]](#manual-Std___HashMap___insert)` to be used with raw hash maps.
- Each operation `T.Raw.f` has an associated well-formedness lemma `T.Raw.WF.f`. For example, `Std.HashMap.Raw.WF.insert` asserts that inserting a new key-value pair into a well-formed raw hash map results in a well-formed raw hash map.

Because the vast majority of use cases do not require them, not all lemmas about raw types are imported by default with the data structures.
It is usually necessary to import `Std.Data.T.RawLemmas` (where `T` is the data structure in question).

A nested inductive type that occurs inside a map or set should be defined in three stages:

1. First, define a raw version of the nested inductive type that uses the raw version of the map or set type. Define any necessary operations.
2. Next, define an inductive predicate that asserts that all maps or sets in the raw nested type are well formed. Show that the operations on the raw type preserve well-formedness.
3. Construct an appropriate interface to the nested inductive type by defining an API that proves well-formedness properties as needed, hiding them from users.

**Example: Nested Inductive Types with Std.HashMap**

This example requires that `Std.Data.HashMap.RawLemmas` is imported.
To keep the code shorter, the `Std` namespace is opened:

```lean
[open]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___open) Std
```

The map of an adventure game may consist of a series of rooms, connected by passages.
Each room has a description, and each passage faces in a particular direction.
This can be represented as a recursive structure.

```lean
structure Maze where
description : [String]](#manual-String___ofByteArray)
passages : [HashMap]](#manual-Std___HashMap) [String]](#manual-String___ofByteArray) Maze
```

This definition is rejected:

```lean
(kernel) application type mismatch
  [DHashMap.Raw.WF]](#manual-Std___DHashMap___Raw___WF___wf) inner
argument has type
  _nested.Std.DHashMap.Raw_3
but function has type
  (DHashMap.Raw String fun x => Maze) → Prop
```

Making this work requires separating the well-formedness predicates from the structure.
The first step is to redefine the type without embedded hash map invariants:

```lean
structure RawMaze where
description : [String]](#manual-String___ofByteArray)
passages : [Std.HashMap.Raw]](#manual-Std___HashMap___Raw___mk) [String]](#manual-String___ofByteArray) [RawMaze]](#manual-RawMaze-_LPAR_in-Nested-Inductive-Types-with--Std___HashMap_RPAR_)
```

The most basic raw maze has no passages:

```lean
def RawMaze.base (description : [String]](#manual-String___ofByteArray)) : [RawMaze]](#manual-RawMaze-_LPAR_in-Nested-Inductive-Types-with--Std___HashMap_RPAR_) where
[description]](#manual-RawMaze___description-_LPAR_in-Nested-Inductive-Types-with--Std___HashMap_RPAR_) := description
[passages]](#manual-RawMaze___passages-_LPAR_in-Nested-Inductive-Types-with--Std___HashMap_RPAR_) := ∅
```

A passage to a further maze can be added to a raw maze using `[RawMaze.insert]](#manual-RawMaze___insert-_LPAR_in-Nested-Inductive-Types-with--Std___HashMap_RPAR_)`:

```lean
def RawMaze.insert (maze : [RawMaze]](#manual-RawMaze-_LPAR_in-Nested-Inductive-Types-with--Std___HashMap_RPAR_))
(direction : [String]](#manual-String___ofByteArray)) (next : [RawMaze]](#manual-RawMaze-_LPAR_in-Nested-Inductive-Types-with--Std___HashMap_RPAR_)) : [RawMaze]](#manual-RawMaze-_LPAR_in-Nested-Inductive-Types-with--Std___HashMap_RPAR_) :=
{ maze with
[passages]](#manual-RawMaze___passages-_LPAR_in-Nested-Inductive-Types-with--Std___HashMap_RPAR_) := maze.[passages]](#manual-RawMaze___passages-_LPAR_in-Nested-Inductive-Types-with--Std___HashMap_RPAR_).insert direction next
}
```

The second step is to define a well-formedness predicate for `[RawMaze]](#manual-RawMaze-_LPAR_in-Nested-Inductive-Types-with--Std___HashMap_RPAR_)` that ensures that each included hash map is well-formed.
If the `[passages]](#manual-RawMaze___passages-_LPAR_in-Nested-Inductive-Types-with--Std___HashMap_RPAR_)` field itself is well-formed, and all raw mazes included in it are well-formed, then a raw maze is well-formed.

```lean
inductive RawMaze.WF : [RawMaze]](#manual-RawMaze-_LPAR_in-Nested-Inductive-Types-with--Std___HashMap_RPAR_) → Prop
| mk {description passages} :
(∀ (dir : [String]](#manual-String___ofByteArray)) v, passages[dir]? = [some]](#manual-Option___none) v → [WF]](#manual-RawMaze___WF-_LPAR_in-Nested-Inductive-Types-with--Std___HashMap_RPAR_) v) →
passages.[WF]](#manual-Std___HashMap___Raw___WF___mk) →
[WF]](#manual-RawMaze___WF-_LPAR_in-Nested-Inductive-Types-with--Std___HashMap_RPAR_) { [description]](#manual-RawMaze___description-_LPAR_in-Nested-Inductive-Types-with--Std___HashMap_RPAR_), [passages]](#manual-RawMaze___passages-_LPAR_in-Nested-Inductive-Types-with--Std___HashMap_RPAR_) := passages }
```

Base mazes are well-formed, and inserting a passage to a well-formed maze into some other well-formed maze produces a well-formed maze:

```lean
theorem RawMaze.base_wf (description : [String]](#manual-String___ofByteArray)) :
[RawMaze.WF]](#manual-RawMaze___WF-_LPAR_in-Nested-Inductive-Types-with--Std___HashMap_RPAR_) ([.base]](#manual-RawMaze___base-_LPAR_in-Nested-Inductive-Types-with--Std___HashMap_RPAR_) description) := bydescription:[String]](#manual-String___ofByteArray)⊢ ([base]](#manual-RawMaze___base-_LPAR_in-Nested-Inductive-Types-with--Std___HashMap_RPAR_) description).[WF]](#manual-RawMaze___WF-_LPAR_in-Nested-Inductive-Types-with--Std___HashMap_RPAR_)
```

Finally, a more friendly interface can be defined that frees users from worrying about well-formedness.
A `Maze` bundles up a `[RawMaze]](#manual-RawMaze-_LPAR_in-Nested-Inductive-Types-with--Std___HashMap_RPAR_)` with a proof that it is well-formed:

```lean
structure Maze where
raw : [RawMaze]](#manual-RawMaze-_LPAR_in-Nested-Inductive-Types-with--Std___HashMap_RPAR_)
wf : raw.[WF]](#manual-RawMaze___WF-_LPAR_in-Nested-Inductive-Types-with--Std___HashMap_RPAR_)
```

#### 20.19.1.3. Suitable Operators for Uniqueness {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Basic-Types--Maps-and-Sets--Library-Design--Suitable-Operators-for-Uniqueness}

Care should be taken when working with data structures to ensure that as many references are unique as possible, which enables Lean to use destructive mutation behind the scenes while maintaining a pure functional interface.
The map and set library provides operators that can be used to maintain uniqueness of references.
In particular, when possible, operations such as `[alter]](#manual-Std___HashMap___alter)` or `[modify]](#manual-Std___HashMap___modify)` should be preferred over explicitly retrieving a value, modifying it, and reinserting it.
These operations avoid creating a second reference to the value during modification.

**Example: Modifying Values in Maps**

```lean
[open]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___open) Std
```

The function `[addAlias]](#manual-addAlias-_LPAR_in-Modifying-Values-in-Maps_RPAR_)` is used to track aliases of a string in some data set.
One way to add an alias is to first look up the existing aliases, defaulting to the empty array, then insert the new alias, and finally save the resulting array in the map:

```lean
def addAlias (aliases : [HashMap]](#manual-Std___HashMap) [String]](#manual-String___ofByteArray) ([Array]](#manual-Array___mk) [String]](#manual-String___ofByteArray)))
(key value : [String]](#manual-String___ofByteArray)) :
[HashMap]](#manual-Std___HashMap) [String]](#manual-String___ofByteArray) ([Array]](#manual-Array___mk) [String]](#manual-String___ofByteArray)) :=
let prior := aliases.[getD]](#manual-Std___HashMap___getD) key #[]
aliases.[insert]](#manual-Std___HashMap___insert) key (prior.[push]](#manual-Array___push) value)
```

This implementation has poor performance characteristics.
Because the map retains a reference to the prior values, the array must be copied rather than mutated.
A better implementation explicitly erases the prior value from the map before modifying it:

```lean
def addAlias' (aliases : [HashMap]](#manual-Std___HashMap) [String]](#manual-String___ofByteArray) ([Array]](#manual-Array___mk) [String]](#manual-String___ofByteArray)))
(key value : [String]](#manual-String___ofByteArray)) :
[HashMap]](#manual-Std___HashMap) [String]](#manual-String___ofByteArray) ([Array]](#manual-Array___mk) [String]](#manual-String___ofByteArray)) :=
let prior := aliases.[getD]](#manual-Std___HashMap___getD) key #[]
let aliases := aliases.[erase]](#manual-Std___HashMap___erase) key
aliases.[insert]](#manual-Std___HashMap___insert) key (prior.[push]](#manual-Array___push) value)
```

Using `[HashMap.alter]](#manual-Std___HashMap___alter)` is even better.
It removes the need to explicitly delete and re-insert the value:

```lean
def addAlias'' (aliases : [HashMap]](#manual-Std___HashMap) [String]](#manual-String___ofByteArray) ([Array]](#manual-Array___mk) [String]](#manual-String___ofByteArray)))
(key value : [String]](#manual-String___ofByteArray)) :
[HashMap]](#manual-Std___HashMap) [String]](#manual-String___ofByteArray) ([Array]](#manual-Array___mk) [String]](#manual-String___ofByteArray)) :=
aliases.[alter]](#manual-Std___HashMap___alter) key fun prior? =>
[some]](#manual-Option___none) ((prior?.[getD]](#manual-Option___getD) #[]).[push]](#manual-Array___push) value)
```

### 20.19.2. Hash Maps {#manual-HashMap}

The declarations in this section should be imported using `import Std.HashMap`.

structure

```lean
[Std.HashMap.{u, v}]](#manual-Std___HashMap) (α : Type u) (β : Type v) [[BEq]](#manual-BEq___mk) α] [[Hashable]](#manual-Hashable___mk) α] :
  Type (max u v)



[Std.HashMap.{u, v}]](#manual-Std___HashMap) (α : Type u)
  (β : Type v) [[BEq]](#manual-BEq___mk) α] [[Hashable]](#manual-Hashable___mk) α] :
  Type (max u v)
```

Hash maps.

This is a simple separate-chaining hash table. The data of the hash map consists of a cached size
and an array of buckets, where each bucket is a linked list of key-value pairs. The number of buckets
is always a power of two. The hash map doubles its size upon inserting an element such that the
number of elements is more than 75% of the number of buckets.

The hash table is backed by an `[Array]](#manual-Array___mk)`. Users should make sure that the hash map is used linearly to
avoid expensive copies.

The hash map uses `==` (provided by the `[BEq]](#manual-BEq___mk)` typeclass) to compare keys and `[hash]](#manual-Hashable___mk)` (provided by
the `[Hashable]](#manual-Hashable___mk)` typeclass) to hash them. To ensure that the operations behave as expected, `==`
should be an equivalence relation and `a == b` should imply `hash a = hash b` (see also the
`[EquivBEq]](#manual-EquivBEq___mk)` and `[LawfulHashable]](#manual-LawfulHashable___mk)` typeclasses). Both of these conditions are automatic if the BEq
instance is lawful, i.e., if `a == b` implies `a = b`.

These hash maps contain a bundled well-formedness invariant, which means that they cannot
be used in nested inductive types. For these use cases, `Std.Data.HashMap.Raw` and
`Std.Data.HashMap.Raw.WF` unbundle the invariant from the hash map. When in doubt, prefer
`HashMap` over `HashMap.Raw`.

Dependent hash maps, in which keys may occur in their values' types, are available as
`Std.Data.DHashMap`.

#### 20.19.2.1. Creation {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Basic-Types--Maps-and-Sets--Hash-Maps--Creation}

def

```lean
[Std.HashMap.emptyWithCapacity.{u, v}]](#manual-Std___HashMap___emptyWithCapacity) {α : Type u} {β : Type v} [[BEq]](#manual-BEq___mk) α]
  [[Hashable]](#manual-Hashable___mk) α] (capacity : [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero) := 8) : [Std.HashMap]](#manual-Std___HashMap) α β



[Std.HashMap.emptyWithCapacity.{u, v}]](#manual-Std___HashMap___emptyWithCapacity)
  {α : Type u} {β : Type v} [[BEq]](#manual-BEq___mk) α]
  [[Hashable]](#manual-Hashable___mk) α] (capacity : [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero) := 8) :
  [Std.HashMap]](#manual-Std___HashMap) α β
```

Creates a new empty hash map. The optional parameter `capacity` can be supplied to presize the
map so that it can hold the given number of mappings without reallocating. It is also possible to
use the empty collection notations `∅` and `{}` to create an empty hash map with the default
capacity.

#### 20.19.2.2. Properties {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Basic-Types--Maps-and-Sets--Hash-Maps--Properties}

def

```lean
[Std.HashMap.size.{u, v}]](#manual-Std___HashMap___size) {α : Type u} {β : Type v} {x✝ : [BEq]](#manual-BEq___mk) α}
```

Returns `[true]](#manual-Bool___false)` if there is a mapping for the given key. There is also a `Prop`-valued version
of this: `a ∈ m` is equivalent to `m.[contains]](#manual-Std___HashMap___contains) a = [true]](#manual-Bool___false)`.

Observe that this is different behavior than for lists: for lists, `∈` uses `=` and `contains` uses
`==` for comparisons, while for hash maps, both use `==`.

If the returned `[Bool]](#manual-Bool___false)` is `[true]](#manual-Bool___false)`, then the returned map is unaltered. If the `[Bool]](#manual-Bool___false)` is `[false]](#manual-Bool___false)`, then
the returned map has a new value inserted.

Equivalent to (but potentially faster than) calling `contains` followed by `insertIfNew`.

Inserts the given mapping into the map. If there is already a mapping for the given key, then both
key and value will be replaced.

Note: this replacement behavior is true for `HashMap`, `DHashMap`, `HashMap.Raw` and `DHashMap.Raw`.
The `insert` function on `HashSet` and `HashSet.Raw` behaves differently: it will return the set
unchanged if a matching key is already present.

Checks whether a key is present in a map, returning the associated value, and inserts a value for
the key if it was not found.

If the returned value is `[some]](#manual-Option___none) v`, then the returned map is unaltered. If it is `[none]](#manual-Option___none)`, then the
returned map has a new value inserted.

Equivalent to (but potentially faster than) calling `get?` followed by `insertIfNew`.

#### 20.19.2.7. Unbundled Variants {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Basic-Types--Maps-and-Sets--Hash-Maps--Unbundled-Variants}

Unbundled maps separate well-formedness proofs from data.
This is primarily useful when defining [nested inductive types]](#manual-raw-data).
To use these variants, import the modules `Std.HashMap.Raw` and `Std.HashMap.RawLemmas`.

structure

```lean
[Std.HashMap.Raw.{u, v}]](#manual-Std___HashMap___Raw___mk) (α : Type u) (β : Type v) : Type (max u v)



[Std.HashMap.Raw.{u, v}]](#manual-Std___HashMap___Raw___mk) (α : Type u)
  (β : Type v) : Type (max u v)
```

Hash maps without a bundled well-formedness invariant, suitable for use in nested
inductive types. The well-formedness invariant is called `Raw.WF`. When in doubt, prefer `HashMap`
over `HashMap.Raw`. Lemmas about the operations on `Std.Data.HashMap.Raw` are available in the
module `Std.Data.HashMap.RawLemmas`.

This is a simple separate-chaining hash table. The data of the hash map consists of a cached size
and an array of buckets, where each bucket is a linked list of key-value pairs. The number of buckets
is always a power of two. The hash map doubles its size upon inserting an element such that the
number of elements is more than 75% of the number of buckets.

The hash table is backed by an `[Array]](#manual-Array___mk)`. Users should make sure that the hash map is used linearly to
avoid expensive copies.

The hash map uses `==` (provided by the `[BEq]](#manual-BEq___mk)` typeclass) to compare keys and `[hash]](#manual-Hashable___mk)` (provided by
the `[Hashable]](#manual-Hashable___mk)` typeclass) to hash them. To ensure that the operations behave as expected, `==`
should be an equivalence relation and `a == b` should imply `hash a = hash b` (see also the
`[EquivBEq]](#manual-EquivBEq___mk)` and `[LawfulHashable]](#manual-LawfulHashable___mk)` typeclasses). Both of these conditions are automatic if the BEq
instance is lawful, i.e., if `a == b` implies `a = b`.

Dependent hash maps, in which keys may occur in their values' types, are available as
`Std.Data.Raw.DHashMap`.

Constructor

```lean
[Std.HashMap.Raw.mk]](#manual-Std___HashMap___Raw___mk).{u, v}
```

Fields

```lean
inner : [Std.DHashMap.Raw]](#manual-Std___DHashMap___Raw___mk) α fun x => β
```

Internal implementation detail of the hash map

structure

```lean
[Std.HashMap.Raw.WF.{u, v}]](#manual-Std___HashMap___Raw___WF___mk) {α : Type u} {β : Type v} [[BEq]](#manual-BEq___mk) α] [[Hashable]](#manual-Hashable___mk) α]
  (m : [Std.HashMap.Raw]](#manual-Std___HashMap___Raw___mk) α β) : Prop



[Std.HashMap.Raw.WF.{u, v}]](#manual-Std___HashMap___Raw___WF___mk) {α : Type u}
  {β : Type v} [[BEq]](#manual-BEq___mk) α] [[Hashable]](#manual-Hashable___mk) α]
  (m : [Std.HashMap.Raw]](#manual-Std___HashMap___Raw___mk) α β) : Prop
```

Well-formedness predicate for hash maps. Users of `HashMap` will not need to interact with this.
Users of `HashMap.Raw` will need to provide proofs of `WF` to lemmas and should use lemmas
`WF.empty` and `WF.insert` (which are always named exactly like the operations they are about) to
show that map operations preserve well-formedness.



### 20.19.3. Dependent Hash Maps {#manual-DHashMap}

The declarations in this section should be imported using `import Std.DHashMap`.

structure

```lean
[Std.DHashMap.{u, v}]](#manual-Std___DHashMap) (α : Type u) (β : α → Type v) [[BEq]](#manual-BEq___mk) α] [[Hashable]](#manual-Hashable___mk) α] :
  Type (max u v)



[Std.DHashMap.{u, v}]](#manual-Std___DHashMap) (α : Type u)
  (β : α → Type v) [[BEq]](#manual-BEq___mk) α] [[Hashable]](#manual-Hashable___mk) α] :
  Type (max u v)
```

Dependent hash maps.

This is a simple separate-chaining hash table. The data of the hash map consists of a cached size
and an array of buckets, where each bucket is a linked list of key-value pairs. The number of buckets
is always a power of two. The hash map doubles its size upon inserting an element such that the
number of elements is more than 75% of the number of buckets.

The hash table is backed by an `[Array]](#manual-Array___mk)`. Users should make sure that the hash map is used linearly to
avoid expensive copies.

The hash map uses `==` (provided by the `[BEq]](#manual-BEq___mk)` typeclass) to compare keys and `[hash]](#manual-Hashable___mk)` (provided by
the `[Hashable]](#manual-Hashable___mk)` typeclass) to hash them. To ensure that the operations behave as expected, `==`
should be an equivalence relation and `a == b` should imply `hash a = hash b` (see also the
`[EquivBEq]](#manual-EquivBEq___mk)` and `[LawfulHashable]](#manual-LawfulHashable___mk)` typeclasses). Both of these conditions are automatic if the BEq
instance is lawful, i.e., if `a == b` implies `a = b`.

These hash maps contain a bundled well-formedness invariant, which means that they cannot
be used in nested inductive types. For these use cases, `[Std.DHashMap.Raw]](#manual-Std___DHashMap___Raw___mk)` and
`[Std.DHashMap.Raw.WF]](#manual-Std___DHashMap___Raw___WF___wf)` unbundle the invariant from the hash map. When in doubt, prefer
`DHashMap` over `DHashMap.Raw`.

For a variant that is more convenient for use in proofs because of extensionalities, see
`[Std.ExtDHashMap]](#manual-Std___ExtDHashMap)` which is defined in the module `Std.Data.ExtDHashMap`.

#### 20.19.3.1. Creation {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Basic-Types--Maps-and-Sets--Dependent-Hash-Maps--Creation}

def

```lean
[Std.DHashMap.emptyWithCapacity.{u, v}]](#manual-Std___DHashMap___emptyWithCapacity) {α : Type u} {β : α → Type v}
  [[BEq]](#manual-BEq___mk) α] [[Hashable]](#manual-Hashable___mk) α] (capacity : [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero) := 8) : [Std.DHashMap]](#manual-Std___DHashMap) α β



[Std.DHashMap.emptyWithCapacity.{u, v}]](#manual-Std___DHashMap___emptyWithCapacity)
  {α : Type u} {β : α → Type v} [[BEq]](#manual-BEq___mk) α]
  [[Hashable]](#manual-Hashable___mk) α] (capacity : [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero) := 8) :
  [Std.DHashMap]](#manual-Std___DHashMap) α β
```

Creates a new empty hash map. The optional parameter `capacity` can be supplied to presize the
map so that it can hold the given number of mappings without reallocating. It is also possible to
use the empty collection notations `∅` and `{}` to create an empty hash map with the default
capacity.

Note that if your `[BEq]](#manual-BEq___mk)` instance is not reflexive or your `[Hashable]](#manual-Hashable___mk)` instance is not
lawful, then it is possible that this function returns `[false]](#manual-Bool___false)` even though is not possible
to get anything out of the hash map.


Internal implementation detail of the hash map

syntaxEquivalence

The relation `[DHashMap.Equiv]](#manual-Std___DHashMap___Equiv___mk)` can also be written with an infix operator, which is scoped to its namespace:

```lean
term ::= ...
    | term ~m term
```

```lean
  {x✝¹ : [Hashable]](#manual-Hashable___mk) α} (m : [Std.DHashMap]](#manual-Std___DHashMap) α β) (a : α) : [Bool]](#manual-Bool___false)

  {x✝¹ : [Hashable]](#manual-Hashable___mk) α}
  (m : [Std.DHashMap]](#manual-Std___DHashMap) α β) (a : α) : [Bool]](#manual-Bool___false)
```

Returns `[true]](#manual-Bool___false)` if there is a mapping for the given key. There is also a `Prop`-valued version
of this: `a ∈ m` is equivalent to `m.[contains]](#manual-Std___DHashMap___contains) a = [true]](#manual-Bool___false)`.

Observe that this is different behavior than for lists: for lists, `∈` uses `=` and `contains` uses
`==` for comparisons, while for hash maps, both use `==`.

Checks whether a key is present in a map and inserts a value for the key if it was not found.

If the returned `[Bool]](#manual-Bool___false)` is `[true]](#manual-Bool___false)`, then the returned map is unaltered. If the `[Bool]](#manual-Bool___false)` is `[false]](#manual-Bool___false)`, then
the returned map has a new value inserted.

Equivalent to (but potentially faster than) calling `contains` followed by `insertIfNew`.

Computes the union of the given hash maps. If a key appears in both maps, the entry contained in
the second argument will appear in the result.

This function always merges the smaller map into the larger map, so the expected runtime is
`O(min(m₁.size, m₂.size))`.
