#### 20.19.3.7. Unbundled Variants {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Basic-Types--Maps-and-Sets--Dependent-Hash-Maps--Unbundled-Variants}

Unbundled maps separate well-formedness proofs from data.
This is primarily useful when defining [nested inductive types]](#manual-raw-data).
To use these variants, import the modules `Std.DHashMap.Raw` and `Std.DHashMap.RawLemmas`.

structure

```lean
[Std.DHashMap.Raw.{u, v}]](#manual-Std___DHashMap___Raw___mk) (α : Type u) (β : α → Type v) : Type (max u v)



[Std.DHashMap.Raw.{u, v}]](#manual-Std___DHashMap___Raw___mk) (α : Type u)
  (β : α → Type v) : Type (max u v)
```

Dependent hash maps without a bundled well-formedness invariant, suitable for use in nested
inductive types. The well-formedness invariant is called `Raw.WF`. When in doubt, prefer `DHashMap`
over `DHashMap.Raw`. Lemmas about the operations on `Std.Data.DHashMap.Raw` are available in the
module `Std.Data.DHashMap.RawLemmas`.

The hash table is backed by an `[Array]](#manual-Array___mk)`. Users should make sure that the hash map is used linearly to
avoid expensive copies.

This is a simple separate-chaining hash table. The data of the hash map consists of a cached size
and an array of buckets, where each bucket is a linked list of key-value pairs. The number of buckets
is always a power of two. The hash map doubles its size upon inserting an element such that the
number of elements is more than 75% of the number of buckets.

The hash map uses `==` (provided by the `[BEq]](#manual-BEq___mk)` typeclass) to compare keys and `[hash]](#manual-Hashable___mk)` (provided by
the `[Hashable]](#manual-Hashable___mk)` typeclass) to hash them. To ensure that the operations behave as expected, `==`
should be an equivalence relation and `a == b` should imply `hash a = hash b` (see also the
`[EquivBEq]](#manual-EquivBEq___mk)` and `[LawfulHashable]](#manual-LawfulHashable___mk)` typeclasses). Both of these conditions are automatic if the BEq
instance is lawful, i.e., if `a == b` implies `a = b`.

Constructor

```lean
[Std.DHashMap.Raw.mk]](#manual-Std___DHashMap___Raw___mk).{u, v}
```

Fields

```lean
size : [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero)
```

The number of mappings present in the hash map

```lean
buckets : [Array]](#manual-Array___mk) (Std.DHashMap.Internal.AssocList α β)
```

Internal implementation detail of the hash map

inductive predicate

```lean
[Std.DHashMap.Raw.WF.{u, v}]](#manual-Std___DHashMap___Raw___WF___wf) {α : Type u} {β : α → Type v} [[BEq]](#manual-BEq___mk) α]
  [[Hashable]](#manual-Hashable___mk) α] : [Std.DHashMap.Raw]](#manual-Std___DHashMap___Raw___mk) α β → Prop



[Std.DHashMap.Raw.WF.{u, v}]](#manual-Std___DHashMap___Raw___WF___wf) {α : Type u}
  {β : α → Type v} [[BEq]](#manual-BEq___mk) α] [[Hashable]](#manual-Hashable___mk) α] :
  [Std.DHashMap.Raw]](#manual-Std___DHashMap___Raw___mk) α β → Prop
```

Well-formedness predicate for hash maps. Users of `DHashMap` will not need to interact with
this. Users of `DHashMap.Raw` will need to provide proofs of `WF` to lemmas and should use lemmas
like `WF.empty` and `WF.insert` (which are always named exactly like the operations they are about)
to show that map operations preserve well-formedness. The constructors of this type are internal
implementation details and should not be accessed by users.

Constructors

### 20.19.4. Extensional Hash Maps {#manual-ExtHashMap}

The declarations in this section should be imported using `import Std.ExtHashMap`.

structure

```lean
[Std.ExtHashMap.{u, v}]](#manual-Std___ExtHashMap) (α : Type u) (β : Type v) [[BEq]](#manual-BEq___mk) α] [[Hashable]](#manual-Hashable___mk) α] :
  Type (max u v)



[Std.ExtHashMap.{u, v}]](#manual-Std___ExtHashMap) (α : Type u)
  (β : Type v) [[BEq]](#manual-BEq___mk) α] [[Hashable]](#manual-Hashable___mk) α] :
  Type (max u v)
```

Hash maps.

This is a simple separate-chaining hash table. The data of the hash map consists of a cached size
and an array of buckets, where each bucket is a linked list of key-value pairs. The number of buckets
is always a power of two. The hash map doubles its size upon inserting an element such that the
number of elements is more than 75% of the number of buckets.

The hash table is backed by an `[Array]](#manual-Array___mk)`. Users should make sure that the hash map is used linearly to
avoid expensive copies.

The hash map uses `==` (provided by the `[BEq]](#manual-BEq___mk)` typeclass) to compare keys and `[hash]](#manual-Hashable___mk)` (provided by
the `[Hashable]](#manual-Hashable___mk)` typeclass) to hash them. To ensure that the operations behave as expected, `==`
should be an equivalence relation and `a == b` should imply `hash a = hash b` (see also the
`[EquivBEq]](#manual-EquivBEq___mk)` and `[LawfulHashable]](#manual-LawfulHashable___mk)` typeclasses). Both of these conditions are automatic if the BEq
instance is lawful, i.e., if `a == b` implies `a = b`.

In contrast to regular hash maps, `[Std.ExtHashMap]](#manual-Std___ExtHashMap)` offers several extensionality lemmas
and therefore has more lemmas about equality of hash maps. This however also makes it lose the
ability to iterate freely over hash maps.

These hash maps contain a bundled well-formedness invariant, which means that they cannot
be used in nested inductive types. For these use cases, `[Std.HashMap.Raw]](#manual-Std___HashMap___Raw___mk)` and
`[Std.HashMap.Raw.WF]](#manual-Std___HashMap___Raw___WF___mk)` unbundle the invariant from the hash map. When in doubt, prefer
`HashMap` or `ExtHashMap` over `HashMap.Raw`.

Dependent hash maps, in which keys may occur in their values' types, are available as
`[Std.ExtDHashMap]](#manual-Std___ExtDHashMap)` in the module `Std.Data.ExtDHashMap`.

#### 20.19.4.1. Creation {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Basic-Types--Maps-and-Sets--Extensional-Hash-Maps--Creation}

def

```lean
[Std.ExtHashMap.emptyWithCapacity.{u, v}]](#manual-Std___ExtHashMap___emptyWithCapacity) {α : Type u} {β : Type v}
  [[BEq]](#manual-BEq___mk) α] [[Hashable]](#manual-Hashable___mk) α] (capacity : [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero) := 8) : [Std.ExtHashMap]](#manual-Std___ExtHashMap) α β



[Std.ExtHashMap.emptyWithCapacity.{u, v}]](#manual-Std___ExtHashMap___emptyWithCapacity)
  {α : Type u} {β : Type v} [[BEq]](#manual-BEq___mk) α]
  [[Hashable]](#manual-Hashable___mk) α] (capacity : [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero) := 8) :
  [Std.ExtHashMap]](#manual-Std___ExtHashMap) α β
```

Creates a new empty hash map. The optional parameter `capacity` can be supplied to presize the
map so that it can hold the given number of mappings without reallocating. It is also possible to
use the empty collection notations `∅` and `{}` to create an empty hash map with the default
capacity.

def

```lean
  {β : Type v} {x✝ : [BEq]](#manual-BEq___mk) α}
  {x✝¹ : [Hashable]](#manual-Hashable___mk) α} [[EquivBEq]](#manual-EquivBEq___mk) α]
  [[LawfulHashable]](#manual-LawfulHashable___mk) α]
  (m : [Std.ExtHashMap]](#manual-Std___ExtHashMap) α β) : [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero)
```

The number of mappings present in the hash map

def

```lean
[Std.ExtHashMap.isEmpty.{u, v}]](#manual-Std___ExtHashMap___isEmpty) {α : Type u} {β : Type v} {x✝ : [BEq]](#manual-BEq___mk) α}
  {x✝¹ : [Hashable]](#manual-Hashable___mk) α} [[EquivBEq]](#manual-EquivBEq___mk) α] [[LawfulHashable]](#manual-LawfulHashable___mk) α]
  (m : [Std.ExtHashMap]](#manual-Std___ExtHashMap) α β) : [Bool]](#manual-Bool___false)



[Std.ExtHashMap.isEmpty.{u, v}]](#manual-Std___ExtHashMap___isEmpty) {α : Type u}
  {β : Type v} {x✝ : [BEq]](#manual-BEq___mk) α}
  {x✝¹ : [Hashable]](#manual-Hashable___mk) α} [[EquivBEq]](#manual-EquivBEq___mk) α]
  [[LawfulHashable]](#manual-LawfulHashable___mk) α]
  (m : [Std.ExtHashMap]](#manual-Std___ExtHashMap) α β) : [Bool]](#manual-Bool___false)
```

Returns `[true]](#manual-Bool___false)` if the hash map contains no mappings.

Note that if your `[BEq]](#manual-BEq___mk)` instance is not reflexive or your `[Hashable]](#manual-Hashable___mk)` instance is not
lawful, then it is possible that this function returns `[false]](#manual-Bool___false)` even though is not possible
to get anything out of the hash map.

#### 20.19.4.3. Queries {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Basic-Types--Maps-and-Sets--Extensional-Hash-Maps--Queries}

def

```lean
[Std.ExtHashMap.contains.{u, v}]](#manual-Std___ExtHashMap___contains) {α : Type u} {β : Type v} {x✝ : [BEq]](#manual-BEq___mk) α}
  {x✝¹ : [Hashable]](#manual-Hashable___mk) α} [[EquivBEq]](#manual-EquivBEq___mk) α] [[LawfulHashable]](#manual-LawfulHashable___mk) α]
  (m : [Std.ExtHashMap]](#manual-Std___ExtHashMap) α β) (a : α) : [Bool]](#manual-Bool___false)



[Std.ExtHashMap.contains.{u, v}]](#manual-Std___ExtHashMap___contains)
  {α : Type u} {β : Type v} {x✝ : [BEq]](#manual-BEq___mk) α}
  {x✝¹ : [Hashable]](#manual-Hashable___mk) α} [[EquivBEq]](#manual-EquivBEq___mk) α]
  [[LawfulHashable]](#manual-LawfulHashable___mk) α]
  (m : [Std.ExtHashMap]](#manual-Std___ExtHashMap) α β) (a : α) : [Bool]](#manual-Bool___false)
```

Returns `[true]](#manual-Bool___false)` if there is a mapping for the given key. There is also a `Prop`-valued version
of this: `a ∈ m` is equivalent to `m.[contains]](#manual-Std___ExtHashMap___contains) a = [true]](#manual-Bool___false)`.

Observe that this is different behavior than for lists: for lists, `∈` uses `=` and `contains` uses
`==` for comparisons, while for hash maps, both use `==`.

def


Inserts the given mapping into the map. If there is already a mapping for the given key, then both
key and value will be replaced.

Note: this replacement behavior is true for `HashMap`, `DHashMap`, `HashMap.Raw` and `DHashMap.Raw`.
The `insert` function on `HashSet` and `HashSet.Raw` behaves differently: it will return the set
unchanged if a matching key is already present.

```lean
  (m : [Std.ExtHashMap]](#manual-Std___ExtHashMap) α β) (l : ρ) :
  [Std.ExtHashMap]](#manual-Std___ExtHashMap) α β
```

Inserts multiple mappings into the hash map by iterating over the given collection and calling
`insert`. If the same key appears multiple times, the last occurrence takes precedence.

Note: this precedence behavior is true for `HashMap`, `DHashMap`, `HashMap.Raw` and `DHashMap.Raw`.
The `insertMany` function on `HashSet` and `HashSet.Raw` behaves differently: it will prefer the first
appearance.

Inserts multiple keys with the value `()` into the hash map by iterating over the given collection
and calling `insertIfNew`. If the same key appears multiple times, the first occurrence takes
precedence.

This is mainly useful to implement `HashSet.insertMany`, so if you are considering using this,
`HashSet` or `HashSet.Raw` might be a better fit for you.

### 20.19.5. Extensional Dependent Hash Maps {#manual-ExtDHashMap}

The declarations in this section should be imported using `import Std.ExtDHashMap`.

structure

```lean
[Std.ExtDHashMap.{u, v}]](#manual-Std___ExtDHashMap) (α : Type u) (β : α → Type v) [[BEq]](#manual-BEq___mk) α]
  [[Hashable]](#manual-Hashable___mk) α] : Type (max u v)



[Std.ExtDHashMap.{u, v}]](#manual-Std___ExtDHashMap) (α : Type u)
  (β : α → Type v) [[BEq]](#manual-BEq___mk) α] [[Hashable]](#manual-Hashable___mk) α] :
  Type (max u v)
```

Extensional dependent hash maps.

This is a simple separate-chaining hash table. The data of the hash map consists of a cached size
and an array of buckets, where each bucket is a linked list of key-value pairs. The number of buckets
is always a power of two. The hash map doubles its size upon inserting an element such that the
number of elements is more than 75% of the number of buckets.

The hash table is backed by an `[Array]](#manual-Array___mk)`. Users should make sure that the hash map is used linearly to
avoid expensive copies.

The hash map uses `==` (provided by the `[BEq]](#manual-BEq___mk)` typeclass) to compare keys and `[hash]](#manual-Hashable___mk)` (provided by
the `[Hashable]](#manual-Hashable___mk)` typeclass) to hash them. To ensure that the operations behave as expected, `==`
must be an equivalence relation and `a == b` must imply `hash a = hash b` (see also the
`[EquivBEq]](#manual-EquivBEq___mk)` and `[LawfulHashable]](#manual-LawfulHashable___mk)` typeclasses). Both of these conditions are automatic if the BEq
instance is lawful, i.e., if `a == b` implies `a = b`.

In contrast to regular dependent hash maps, `[Std.ExtDHashMap]](#manual-Std___ExtDHashMap)` offers several extensionality lemmas
and therefore has more lemmas about equality of hash maps. This however also makes it lose the
ability to iterate freely over the hash map.

These hash maps contain a bundled well-formedness invariant, which means that they cannot
be used in nested inductive types. For these use cases, `[Std.DHashMap.Raw]](#manual-Std___DHashMap___Raw___mk)` and
`[Std.DHashMap.Raw.WF]](#manual-Std___DHashMap___Raw___WF___wf)` unbundle the invariant from the hash map. When in doubt, prefer
`DHashMap` over `DHashMap.Raw`.

#### 20.19.5.1. Creation {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Basic-Types--Maps-and-Sets--Extensional-Dependent-Hash-Maps--Creation}

def

```lean
[Std.ExtDHashMap.emptyWithCapacity.{u, v}]](#manual-Std___ExtDHashMap___emptyWithCapacity) {α : Type u} {β : α → Type v}
  [[BEq]](#manual-BEq___mk) α] [[Hashable]](#manual-Hashable___mk) α] (capacity : [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero) := 8) : [Std.ExtDHashMap]](#manual-Std___ExtDHashMap) α β



[Std.ExtDHashMap.emptyWithCapacity.{u, v}]](#manual-Std___ExtDHashMap___emptyWithCapacity)
  {α : Type u} {β : α → Type v} [[BEq]](#manual-BEq___mk) α]
  [[Hashable]](#manual-Hashable___mk) α] (capacity : [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero) := 8) :
  [Std.ExtDHashMap]](#manual-Std___ExtDHashMap) α β
```

Creates a new empty hash map. The optional parameter `capacity` can be supplied to presize the
map so that it can hold the given number of mappings without reallocating. It is also possible to
use the empty collection notations `∅` and `{}` to create an empty hash map with the default
capacity.

Note that if your `[BEq]](#manual-BEq___mk)` instance is not reflexive or your `[Hashable]](#manual-Hashable___mk)` instance is not
lawful, then it is possible that this function returns `[false]](#manual-Bool___false)` even though is not possible
to get anything out of the hash map.

Returns `[true]](#manual-Bool___false)` if there is a mapping for the given key. There is also a `Prop`-valued version
of this: `a ∈ m` is equivalent to `m.[contains]](#manual-Std___ExtDHashMap___contains) a = [true]](#manual-Bool___false)`.

Observe that this is different behavior than for lists: for lists, `∈` uses `=` and `contains` uses
`==` for comparisons, while for hash maps, both use `==`.

`insert`. If the same key appears multiple times, the last occurrence takes precedence.

Note: this precedence behavior is true for `HashMap`, `DHashMap`, `HashMap.Raw` and `DHashMap.Raw`.
The `insertMany` function on `HashSet` and `HashSet.Raw` behaves differently: it will prefer the first
appearance.

### 20.19.6. Hash Sets {#manual-HashSet}

structure

```lean
[Std.HashSet.{u}]](#manual-Std___HashSet___mk) (α : Type u) [[BEq]](#manual-BEq___mk) α] [[Hashable]](#manual-Hashable___mk) α] : Type u



[Std.HashSet.{u}]](#manual-Std___HashSet___mk) (α : Type u) [[BEq]](#manual-BEq___mk) α]
  [[Hashable]](#manual-Hashable___mk) α] : Type u
```

Hash sets.

This is a simple separate-chaining hash table. The data of the hash set consists of a cached size
and an array of buckets, where each bucket is a linked list of keys. The number of buckets
is always a power of two. The hash set doubles its size upon inserting an element such that the
number of elements is more than 75% of the number of buckets.

The hash table is backed by an `[Array]](#manual-Array___mk)`. Users should make sure that the hash set is used linearly to
avoid expensive copies.

The hash set uses `==` (provided by the `[BEq]](#manual-BEq___mk)` typeclass) to compare elements and `[hash]](#manual-Hashable___mk)` (provided by
the `[Hashable]](#manual-Hashable___mk)` typeclass) to hash them. To ensure that the operations behave as expected, `==`
should be an equivalence relation and `a == b` should imply `hash a = hash b` (see also the
`[EquivBEq]](#manual-EquivBEq___mk)` and `[LawfulHashable]](#manual-LawfulHashable___mk)` typeclasses). Both of these conditions are automatic if the BEq
instance is lawful, i.e., if `a == b` implies `a = b`.

These hash sets contain a bundled well-formedness invariant, which means that they cannot
be used in nested inductive types. For these use cases, `Std.Data.HashSet.Raw` and
`Std.Data.HashSet.Raw.WF` unbundle the invariant from the hash set. When in doubt, prefer
`HashSet` over `HashSet.Raw`.


capacity.

this: `a ∈ m` is equivalent to `m.[contains]](#manual-Std___HashSet___contains) a = [true]](#manual-Bool___false)`.

Observe that this is different behavior than for lists: for lists, `∈` uses `=` and `contains` use
`==` for comparisons, while for hash sets, both use `==`.

Note: this non-replacement behavior is true for `HashSet` and `HashSet.Raw`.
The `insert` function on `HashMap`, `DHashMap`, `HashMap.Raw` and `DHashMap.Raw` behaves
differently: it will overwrite an existing mapping.

`HashMap`, `DHashMap`, `HashMap.Raw` and `DHashMap.Raw` behaves differently: it will prefer the last

#### 20.19.6.7. Unbundled Variants {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Basic-Types--Maps-and-Sets--Hash-Sets--Unbundled-Variants}

Unbundled maps separate well-formedness proofs from data.
This is primarily useful when defining [nested inductive types]](#manual-raw-data).
To use these variants, import the modules `Std.HashSet.Raw` and `Std.HashSet.RawLemmas`.

structure

```lean
[Std.HashSet.Raw.{u}]](#manual-Std___HashSet___Raw___mk) (α : Type u) : Type u



[Std.HashSet.Raw.{u}]](#manual-Std___HashSet___Raw___mk) (α : Type u) : Type u
```

Hash sets without a bundled well-formedness invariant, suitable for use in nested
inductive types. The well-formedness invariant is called `Raw.WF`. When in doubt, prefer `HashSet`
over `HashSet.Raw`. Lemmas about the operations on `Std.Data.HashSet.Raw` are available in the
module `Std.Data.HashSet.RawLemmas`.

This is a simple separate-chaining hash table. The data of the hash set consists of a cached size
and an array of buckets, where each bucket is a linked list of keys. The number of buckets
is always a power of two. The hash set doubles its size upon inserting an element such that the
number of elements is more than 75% of the number of buckets.

The hash table is backed by an `[Array]](#manual-Array___mk)`. Users should make sure that the hash set is used linearly to
avoid expensive copies.

The hash set uses `==` (provided by the `[BEq]](#manual-BEq___mk)` typeclass) to compare elements and `[hash]](#manual-Hashable___mk)` (provided by
the `[Hashable]](#manual-Hashable___mk)` typeclass) to hash them. To ensure that the operations behave as expected, `==`
should be an equivalence relation and `a == b` should imply `hash a = hash b` (see also the
`[EquivBEq]](#manual-EquivBEq___mk)` and `[LawfulHashable]](#manual-LawfulHashable___mk)` typeclasses). Both of these conditions are automatic if the BEq
instance is lawful, i.e., if `a == b` implies `a = b`.

Constructor

```lean
[Std.HashSet.Raw.mk]](#manual-Std___HashSet___Raw___mk).{u}
```

Fields

```lean
inner : [Std.HashMap.Raw]](#manual-Std___HashMap___Raw___mk) α [Unit]](#manual-Unit)
```

Internal implementation detail of the hash set.

structure

```lean
[Std.HashSet.Raw.WF.{u}]](#manual-Std___HashSet___Raw___WF___mk) {α : Type u} [[BEq]](#manual-BEq___mk) α] [[Hashable]](#manual-Hashable___mk) α]
  (m : [Std.HashSet.Raw]](#manual-Std___HashSet___Raw___mk) α) : Prop

  [[BEq]](#manual-BEq___mk) α] [[Hashable]](#manual-Hashable___mk) α]
  (m : [Std.HashSet.Raw]](#manual-Std___HashSet___Raw___mk) α) : Prop
```

Well-formedness predicate for hash sets. Users of `HashSet` will not need to interact with this.
Users of `HashSet.Raw` will need to provide proofs of `WF` to lemmas and should use lemmas like
`WF.empty` and `WF.insert` (which are always named exactly like the operations they are about) to
show that set operations preserve well-formedness.


structure

Hash sets.

This is a simple separate-chaining hash table. The data of the hash set consists of a cached size
and an array of buckets, where each bucket is a linked list of keys. The number of buckets
is always a power of two. The hash set doubles its size upon inserting an element such that the
number of elements is more than 75% of the number of buckets.

The hash table is backed by an `[Array]](#manual-Array___mk)`. Users should make sure that the hash set is used linearly to
avoid expensive copies.

The hash set uses `==` (provided by the `[BEq]](#manual-BEq___mk)` typeclass) to compare elements and `[hash]](#manual-Hashable___mk)` (provided by
the `[Hashable]](#manual-Hashable___mk)` typeclass) to hash them. To ensure that the operations behave as expected, `==`
should be an equivalence relation and `a == b` should imply `hash a = hash b` (see also the
`[EquivBEq]](#manual-EquivBEq___mk)` and `[LawfulHashable]](#manual-LawfulHashable___mk)` typeclasses). Both of these conditions are automatic if the BEq
instance is lawful, i.e., if `a == b` implies `a = b`.

In contrast to regular hash sets, `[Std.ExtHashSet]](#manual-Std___ExtHashSet___mk)` offers several extensionality lemmas
and therefore has more lemmas about equality of hash maps. This however also makes it lose the
ability to iterate freely over hash sets.

These hash sets contain a bundled well-formedness invariant, which means that they cannot
be used in nested inductive types. For these use cases, `[Std.HashSet.Raw]](#manual-Std___HashSet___Raw___mk)` and
`[Std.HashSet.Raw.WF]](#manual-Std___HashSet___Raw___WF___mk)` unbundle the invariant from the hash set. When in doubt, prefer
`HashSet` or `ExtHashSet` over `HashSet.Raw`.

### 20.19.8. Tree-Based Maps {#manual-TreeMap}

The declarations in this section should be imported using `import Std.TreeMap`.

structure

```lean
[Std.TreeMap.{u, v}]](#manual-Std___TreeMap) (α : Type u) (β : Type v)
  (cmp : α → α → [Ordering]](#manual-Ordering___lt) := by exact compare) : Type (max u v)



[Std.TreeMap.{u, v}]](#manual-Std___TreeMap) (α : Type u)
  (β : Type v)
  (cmp : α → α → [Ordering]](#manual-Ordering___lt) := by
    exact compare) :
  Type (max u v)
```

Tree maps.

A tree map stores an assignment of keys to values. It depends on a comparator function that
defines an ordering on the keys and provides efficient order-dependent queries, such as retrieval
of the minimum or maximum.

To ensure that the operations behave as expected, the comparator function `cmp` should satisfy
certain laws that ensure a consistent ordering:

- If `a` is less than (or equal) to `b`, then `b` is greater than (or equal) to `a`
  and vice versa (see the `OrientedCmp` typeclass).
- If `a` is less than or equal to `b` and `b` is, in turn, less than or equal to `c`, then `a`
  is less than or equal to `c` (see the `TransCmp` typeclass).

Keys for which `cmp a b = [Ordering.eq]](#manual-Ordering___lt)` are considered the same, i.e., there can be only one entry
with key either `a` or `b` in a tree map. Looking up either `a` or `b` always yields the same entry,
if any is present.

To avoid expensive copies, users should make sure that the tree map is used linearly.

Internally, the tree maps are represented as size-bounded trees, a type of self-balancing binary
search tree with efficient order statistic lookups.

For use in proofs, the type `Std.ExtTreeMap` of extensional tree maps should be preferred. This
type comes with several extensionality lemmas and provides the same functions but requires a
`TransCmp` instance to work with.

These tree maps contain a bundled well-formedness invariant, which means that they cannot
be used in nested inductive types. For these use cases, `[Std.TreeMap.Raw]](#manual-Std___TreeMap___Raw___mk)` and
`[Std.TreeMap.Raw.WF]](#manual-Std___TreeMap___Raw___WF___mk)` unbundle the invariant from the tree map. When in doubt, prefer
`TreeMap` over `TreeMap.Raw`.

```lean
  (l : [Std.TreeMap]](#manual-Std___TreeMap) α β cmp) (a : α) : [Bool]](#manual-Bool___false)
```

Returns `[true]](#manual-Bool___false)` if there is a mapping for the given key `a` or a key that is equal to `a` according
to the comparator `cmp`. There is also a `Prop`-valued version
of this: `a ∈ t` is equivalent to `t.contains a = [true]](#manual-Bool___false)`.

Observe that this is different behavior than for lists: for lists, `∈` uses `=` and `contains` uses
`==` for equality checks, while for tree maps, both use the given comparator `cmp`.

Checks whether a key is present in a map and inserts a value for the key if it was not found.
If the returned `[Bool]](#manual-Bool___false)` is `[true]](#manual-Bool___false)`, then the returned map is unaltered. If the `[Bool]](#manual-Bool___false)` is `[false]](#manual-Bool___false)`,
then the returned map has a new value inserted.

Equivalent to (but potentially faster than) calling `contains` followed by `insertIfNew`.

Checks whether a key is present in a map, returning the associated value, and inserts a value for
the key if it was not found.

If the returned value is `[some]](#manual-Option___none) v`, then the returned map is unaltered. If it is `[none]](#manual-Option___none)`, then the
returned map has a new value inserted.

Equivalent to (but potentially faster than) calling `get?` followed by `insertIfNew`.

Uses the `LawfulEqCmp` instance to cast the retrieved value to the correct type.

Inserts multiple mappings into the tree map by iterating over the given collection and calling
`insert`. If the same key appears multiple times, the last occurrence takes precedence.

Note: this precedence behavior is true for `TreeMap`, `DTreeMap`, `TreeMap.Raw` and `DTreeMap.Raw`.
The `insertMany` function on `TreeSet` and `TreeSet.Raw` behaves differently: it will prefer the first
appearance.

```lean
  [Std.TreeMap]](#manual-Std___TreeMap) α β cmp
```

Returns a map that contains all mappings of `t₁` and `t₂`. In case that both maps contain the
same key `k` with respect to `cmp`, the provided function is used to determine the new value from
the respective values in `t₁` and `t₂`.

This function ensures that `t₁` is used linearly. It also uses the individual values in `t₁`
linearly if the merge function uses the second argument (i.e. the first of type `β a`) linearly.
Hence, as long as `t₁` is unshared, the performance characteristics follow the following imperative
description: Iterate over all mappings in `t₂`, inserting them into `t₁` if `t₁` does not contain a
conflicting mapping yet. If `t₁` does contain a conflicting mapping, use the given merge function to
merge the mapping in `t₂` into the mapping in `t₁`. Then return `t₁`.

Hence, the runtime of this method scales logarithmically in the size of `t₁` and linearly in the size of
`t₂` as long as `t₁` is unshared.

##### 20.19.8.6.1. Unbundled Variants {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Basic-Types--Maps-and-Sets--Tree-Based-Maps--Conversion--Unbundled-Variants}

Unbundled maps separate well-formedness proofs from data.
This is primarily useful when defining [nested inductive types]](#manual-raw-data).
To use these variants, import the module `Std.TreeMap.Raw`.

structure

```lean
[Std.TreeMap.Raw.{u, v}]](#manual-Std___TreeMap___Raw___mk) (α : Type u) (β : Type v)
  (cmp : α → α → [Ordering]](#manual-Ordering___lt) := by exact compare) : Type (max u v)



[Std.TreeMap.Raw.{u, v}]](#manual-Std___TreeMap___Raw___mk) (α : Type u)
  (β : Type v)
  (cmp : α → α → [Ordering]](#manual-Ordering___lt) := by
    exact compare) :
  Type (max u v)
```

Tree maps without a bundled well-formedness invariant, suitable for use in nested
inductive types. The well-formedness invariant is called `Raw.WF`. When in doubt, prefer `TreeMap`
over `TreeMap.Raw`. Lemmas about the operations on `[Std.TreeMap.Raw]](#manual-Std___TreeMap___Raw___mk)` are available in the
module `Std.Data.TreeMap.Raw.Lemmas`.

A tree map stores an assignment of keys to values. It depends on a comparator function that
defines an ordering on the keys and provides efficient order-dependent queries, such as retrieval
of the minimum or maximum.

To ensure that the operations behave as expected, the comparator function `cmp` should satisfy
certain laws that ensure a consistent ordering:

- If `a` is less than (or equal) to `b`, then `b` is greater than (or equal) to `a`
  and vice versa (see the `OrientedCmp` typeclass).
- If `a` is less than or equal to `b` and `b` is, in turn, less than or equal to `c`, then `a`
  is less than or equal to `c` (see the `TransCmp` typeclass).

Keys for which `cmp a b = [Ordering.eq]](#manual-Ordering___lt)` are considered the same, i.e., there can be only one entry
with key either `a` or `b` in a tree map. Looking up either `a` or `b` always yields the same entry,
if any is present.

To avoid expensive copies, users should make sure that the tree map is used linearly.

Internally, the tree maps are represented as size-bounded trees, a type of self-balancing binary
search tree with efficient order statistic lookups.

```lean
[Std.TreeMap.Raw.mk]](#manual-Std___TreeMap___Raw___mk).{u, v}
```


structure

### 20.19.9. Dependent Tree-Based Maps {#manual-DTreeMap}

The declarations in this section should be imported using `import Std.DTreeMap`.

structure

```lean
[Std.DTreeMap.{u, v}]](#manual-Std___DTreeMap) (α : Type u) (β : α → Type v)
  (cmp : α → α → [Ordering]](#manual-Ordering___lt) := by exact compare) : Type (max u v)



[Std.DTreeMap.{u, v}]](#manual-Std___DTreeMap) (α : Type u)
  (β : α → Type v)
  (cmp : α → α → [Ordering]](#manual-Ordering___lt) := by
    exact compare) :
  Type (max u v)
```

Dependent tree maps.

A tree map stores an assignment of keys to values. It depends on a comparator function that
defines an ordering on the keys and provides efficient order-dependent queries, such as retrieval
of the minimum or maximum.

To ensure that the operations behave as expected, the comparator function `cmp` should satisfy
certain laws that ensure a consistent ordering:

- If `a` is less than (or equal) to `b`, then `b` is greater than (or equal) to `a`
  and vice versa (see the `OrientedCmp` typeclass).
- If `a` is less than or equal to `b` and `b` is, in turn, less than or equal to `c`, then `a`
  is less than or equal to `c` (see the `TransCmp` typeclass).

Keys for which `cmp a b = [Ordering.eq]](#manual-Ordering___lt)` are considered the same, i.e., there can be only one entry
with key either `a` or `b` in a tree map. Looking up either `a` or `b` always yields the same entry,
if any is present. The `get` operations of the *dependent* tree map additionally require a
`LawfulEqCmp` instance to ensure that `cmp a b = [.eq]](#manual-Ordering___lt)` always implies `a = b`, so that their
respective value types are equal.

To avoid expensive copies, users should make sure that the tree map is used linearly.

Internally, the tree maps are represented as size-bounded trees, a type of self-balancing binary
search tree with efficient order statistic lookups.

For use in proofs, the type `Std.ExtDTreeMap` of extensional dependent tree maps should be
preferred. This type comes with several extensionality lemmas and provides the same functions but
requires a `TransCmp` instance to work with.

These tree maps contain a bundled well-formedness invariant, which means that they cannot
be used in nested inductive types. For these use cases, `[Std.DTreeMap.Raw]](#manual-Std___DTreeMap___Raw___mk)` and
`[Std.DTreeMap.Raw.WF]](#manual-Std___DTreeMap___Raw___WF___mk)` unbundle the invariant from the tree map. When in doubt, prefer
`DTreeMap` over `DTreeMap.Raw`.

#### 20.19.9.7. Unbundled Variants {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Basic-Types--Maps-and-Sets--Dependent-Tree-Based-Maps--Unbundled-Variants}

Unbundled maps separate well-formedness proofs from data.
This is primarily useful when defining [nested inductive types]](#manual-raw-data).
To use these variants, import the module `Std.DTreeMap.Raw`.

structure

```lean
[Std.DTreeMap.Raw.{u, v}]](#manual-Std___DTreeMap___Raw___mk) (α : Type u) (β : α → Type v)
  (_cmp : α → α → [Ordering]](#manual-Ordering___lt) := by exact compare) : Type (max u v)



[Std.DTreeMap.Raw.{u, v}]](#manual-Std___DTreeMap___Raw___mk) (α : Type u)
  (β : α → Type v)
  (_cmp : α → α → [Ordering]](#manual-Ordering___lt) := by
    exact compare) :
  Type (max u v)
```

Dependent tree maps without a bundled well-formedness invariant, suitable for use in nested
inductive types. The well-formedness invariant is called `Raw.WF`. When in doubt, prefer `DTreeMap`
over `DTreeMap.Raw`. Lemmas about the operations on `[Std.DTreeMap.Raw]](#manual-Std___DTreeMap___Raw___mk)` are available in the
module `Std.Data.DTreeMap.Raw.Lemmas`.

A tree map stores an assignment of keys to values. It depends on a comparator function that
defines an ordering on the keys and provides efficient order-dependent queries, such as retrieval
of the minimum or maximum.

To ensure that the operations behave as expected, the comparator function `cmp` should satisfy
certain laws that ensure a consistent ordering:

- If `a` is less than (or equal) to `b`, then `b` is greater than (or equal) to `a`
  and vice versa (see the `OrientedCmp` typeclass).
- If `a` is less than or equal to `b` and `b` is, in turn, less than or equal to `c`, then `a`
  is less than or equal to `c` (see the `TransCmp` typeclass).

Keys for which `cmp a b = [Ordering.eq]](#manual-Ordering___lt)` are considered the same, i.e., there can be only one entry
with key either `a` or `b` in a tree map. Looking up either `a` or `b` always yields the same entry,
if any is present. The `get` operations of the *dependent* tree map additionally require a
`LawfulEqCmp` instance to ensure that `cmp a b = .eq` always implies `a = b`, so that their
respective value types are equal.

To avoid expensive copies, users should make sure that the tree map is used linearly.

Internally, the tree maps are represented as size-bounded trees, a type of self-balancing binary
search tree with efficient order statistic lookups.

Constructor

```lean
[Std.DTreeMap.Raw.mk]](#manual-Std___DTreeMap___Raw___mk).{u, v}
```

Fields

```lean
inner : Std.DTreeMap.Internal.Impl α β
```

Internal implementation detail of the tree map.

structure

```lean
[Std.DTreeMap.Raw.WF.{u, v}]](#manual-Std___DTreeMap___Raw___WF___mk) {α : Type u} {β : α → Type v}
  {cmp : α → α → [Ordering]](#manual-Ordering___lt)} (t : [Std.DTreeMap.Raw]](#manual-Std___DTreeMap___Raw___mk) α β cmp) : Prop



[Std.DTreeMap.Raw.WF.{u, v}]](#manual-Std___DTreeMap___Raw___WF___mk) {α : Type u}
  {β : α → Type v}
  {cmp : α → α → [Ordering]](#manual-Ordering___lt)}
  (t : [Std.DTreeMap.Raw]](#manual-Std___DTreeMap___Raw___mk) α β cmp) : Prop
```

Well-formedness predicate for tree maps. Users of `DTreeMap` will not need to interact with
this. Users of `DTreeMap.Raw` will need to provide proofs of `WF` to lemmas and should use lemmas
like `WF.empty` and `WF.insert` (which are always named exactly like the operations they are about)
to show that map operations preserve well-formedness. The constructors of this type are internal
implementation details and should not be accessed by users.



### 20.19.10. Tree-Based Sets {#manual-TreeSet}

structure

```lean
[Std.TreeSet.{u}]](#manual-Std___TreeSet) (α : Type u)
  (cmp : α → α → [Ordering]](#manual-Ordering___lt) := by exact compare) : Type u



[Std.TreeSet.{u}]](#manual-Std___TreeSet) (α : Type u)
  (cmp : α → α → [Ordering]](#manual-Ordering___lt) := by
    exact compare) :
  Type u
```

Tree sets.

A tree set stores elements of a certain type in a certain order. It depends on a comparator function
that defines an ordering on the keys and provides efficient order-dependent queries, such as
retrieval of the minimum or maximum.

To ensure that the operations behave as expected, the comparator function `cmp` should satisfy
certain laws that ensure a consistent ordering:

- If `a` is less than (or equal) to `b`, then `b` is greater than (or equal) to `a`
  and vice versa (see the `OrientedCmp` typeclass).
- If `a` is less than or equal to `b` and `b` is, in turn, less than or equal to `c`, then `a`
  is less than or equal to `c` (see the `TransCmp` typeclass).

Keys for which `cmp a b = [Ordering.eq]](#manual-Ordering___lt)` are considered the same, i.e., there can be only one of them
be contained in a single tree set at the same time.

To avoid expensive copies, users should make sure that the tree set is used linearly.

Internally, the tree sets are represented as size-bounded trees, a type of self-balancing binary
search tree with efficient order statistic lookups.

For use in proofs, the type `Std.ExtTreeSet` of extensional tree sets should be preferred. This
type comes with several extensionality lemmas and provides the same functions but requires a
`TransCmp` instance to work with.

These tree sets contain a bundled well-formedness invariant, which means that they cannot
be used in nested inductive types. For these use cases, `[Std.TreeSet.Raw]](#manual-Std___TreeSet___Raw___mk)` and
`[Std.TreeSet.Raw.WF]](#manual-Std___TreeSet___Raw___WF___mk)` unbundle the invariant from the tree set. When in doubt, prefer
`TreeSet` over `TreeSet.Raw`.


Creates a new empty tree set. It is also possible and recommended to
use the empty collection notations `∅` and `{}` to create an empty tree set. `[simp]](#manual-simp)` replaces

#### 20.19.10.3. Queries {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Basic-Types--Maps-and-Sets--Tree-Based-Sets--Queries}

def

```lean
[Std.TreeSet.contains.{u}]](#manual-Std___TreeSet___contains) {α : Type u} {cmp : α → α → [Ordering]](#manual-Ordering___lt)}
  (l : [Std.TreeSet]](#manual-Std___TreeSet) α cmp) (a : α) : [Bool]](#manual-Bool___false)



[Std.TreeSet.contains.{u}]](#manual-Std___TreeSet___contains) {α : Type u}
  {cmp : α → α → [Ordering]](#manual-Ordering___lt)}
  (l : [Std.TreeSet]](#manual-Std___TreeSet) α cmp) (a : α) : [Bool]](#manual-Bool___false)
```

Returns `[true]](#manual-Bool___false)` if `a`, or an element equal to `a` according to the comparator `cmp`, is contained
in the set. There is also a `Prop`-valued version of this: `a ∈ t` is equivalent to
`t.contains a = [true]](#manual-Bool___false)`.

Observe that this is different behavior than for lists: for lists, `∈` uses `=` and `contains` uses
`==` for equality checks, while for tree sets, both use the given comparator `cmp`.

def

```lean
[Std.TreeSet.get.{u}]](#manual-Std___TreeSet___get) {α : Type u} {cmp : α → α → [Ordering]](#manual-Ordering___lt)}
  (t : [Std.TreeSet]](#manual-Std___TreeSet) α cmp) (a : α) (h : a ∈ t) : α



[Std.TreeSet.get.{u}]](#manual-Std___TreeSet___get) {α : Type u}
  {cmp : α → α → [Ordering]](#manual-Ordering___lt)}
  (t : [Std.TreeSet]](#manual-Std___TreeSet) α cmp) (a : α)
  (h : a ∈ t) : α
```

Retrieves the key from the set that matches `a`. Ensures that such a key exists by requiring a proof
of `a ∈ m`. The result is guaranteed to be pointer equal to the key in the set.

##### 20.19.10.6.1. Unbundled Variants {#manual-The-Lean-Language-Reference--Basic-Types--Maps-and-Sets--Tree-Based-Sets--Conversion--Unbundled-Variants}

Unbundled sets separate well-formedness proofs from data.
This is primarily useful when defining [nested inductive types]](#manual-raw-data).
To use these variants, import the module `Std.TreeSet.Raw`.

structure

```lean
[Std.TreeSet.Raw.{u}]](#manual-Std___TreeSet___Raw___mk) (α : Type u)
  (cmp : α → α → [Ordering]](#manual-Ordering___lt) := by exact compare) : Type u



[Std.TreeSet.Raw.{u}]](#manual-Std___TreeSet___Raw___mk) (α : Type u)
  (cmp : α → α → [Ordering]](#manual-Ordering___lt) := by
    exact compare) :
  Type u
```

Tree sets without a bundled well-formedness invariant, suitable for use in nested
inductive types. The well-formedness invariant is called `Raw.WF`. When in doubt, prefer `TreeSet`
over `TreeSet.Raw`. Lemmas about the operations on `[Std.TreeSet.Raw]](#manual-Std___TreeSet___Raw___mk)` are available in the
module `Std.Data.TreeSet.Raw.Lemmas`.

A tree set stores elements of a certain type in a certain order. It depends on a comparator function
that defines an ordering on the keys and provides efficient order-dependent queries, such as
retrieval of the minimum or maximum.

To ensure that the operations behave as expected, the comparator function `cmp` should satisfy
certain laws that ensure a consistent ordering:

- If `a` is less than (or equal) to `b`, then `b` is greater than (or equal) to `a`
  and vice versa (see the `OrientedCmp` typeclass).
- If `a` is less than or equal to `b` and `b` is, in turn, less than or equal to `c`, then `a`
  is less than or equal to `c` (see the `TransCmp` typeclass).

Keys for which `cmp a b = [Ordering.eq]](#manual-Ordering___lt)` are considered the same, i.e only one of them
can be contained in a single tree set at the same time.

To avoid expensive copies, users should make sure that the tree set is used linearly.

Internally, the tree sets are represented as size-bounded trees, a type of self-balancing binary
search tree with efficient order statistic lookups.

```lean
[Std.TreeSet.Raw.mk]](#manual-Std___TreeSet___Raw___mk).{u}
```

Fields

```lean

```

```lean
  (t : [Std.TreeSet.Raw]](#manual-Std___TreeSet___Raw___mk) α cmp) : Prop

  {cmp : α → α → [Ordering]](#manual-Ordering___lt)}
```

this. Users of `TreeSet.Raw` will need to provide proofs of `WF` to lemmas and should use lemmas
like `WF.empty` and `WF.insert` (which are always named exactly like the operations they are about)
to show that set operations preserve well-formedness. The constructors of this type are internal
implementation details and should not be accessed by users.

## Basic Types — 20.20. Subtypes {#manual-basic-types-2020-subtypes}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Subtypes/

The structure `[Subtype]](#manual-Subtype___mk)` represents the elements of a type that satisfy some predicate.
They are used pervasively both in mathematics and in programming; in mathematics, they are used similarly to subsets, while in programming, they allow information that is known about a value to be represented in a way that is visible to Lean's logic.

Syntactically, an element of a `[Subtype]](#manual-Subtype___mk)` resembles a tuple of the base type's element and the proof that it satisfies the proposition.
They differ from dependent pair types (`[Sigma]](#manual-Sigma___mk)`) in that the second element is a proof of a proposition rather than data, and from existential quantification in that the entire `[Subtype]](#manual-Subtype___mk)` is a type rather than a proposition.
Even though they are pairs syntactically, `[Subtype]](#manual-Subtype___mk)` should really be thought of as elements of the base type with associated proof obligations.

Subtypes are [trivial wrappers]](#manual-inductive-types-trivial-wrappers).
They are thus represented identically to the base type in compiled code.

structure

```lean
[Subtype.{u}]](#manual-Subtype___mk) {α : Sort u} (p : α → Prop) : Sort (max 1 u)



[Subtype.{u}]](#manual-Subtype___mk) {α : Sort u} (p : α → Prop) :
  Sort (max 1 u)
```

All the elements of a type that satisfy a predicate.

`[Subtype]](#manual-Subtype___mk) p`, usually written `{ x : α // p x }` or `{ x // p x }`, contains all elements `x : α` for
which `p x` is true. Its constructor is a pair of the value and the proof that it satisfies the
predicate. In run-time code, `{ x : α // p x }` is represented identically to `α`.

There is a coercion from `{ x : α // p x }` to `α`, so elements of a subtype may be used where the
underlying type is expected.

Examples:

- `{ n : [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero) // n % 2 = 0 }` is the type of even numbers.
- `{ xs : [Array]](#manual-Array___mk) [String]](#manual-String___ofByteArray) // xs.[size]](#manual-Array___size) = 5 }` is the type of arrays with five `[String]](#manual-String___ofByteArray)`s.
- Given `xs : List α`, `List { x : α // x ∈ xs }` is the type of lists in which all elements are
  contained in `xs`.

Conventions for notations in identifiers:

- The recommended spelling of `{ x // p x }` in identifiers is `subtype`.

Constructor

```lean
[Subtype.mk]](#manual-Subtype___mk).{u}
```

Fields

```lean
val : α
```

The value in the underlying type that satisfies the predicate.

```lean
property : p self.[val]](#manual-Subtype___mk)
```

The proof that `val` satisfies the predicate `p`.

syntaxSubtypes

```lean
term ::= ...
    | { ident : term // term }
```

`{ x : α // p }` is a notation for `[Subtype]](#manual-Subtype___mk) fun (x : α) => p`.

The type ascription may be omitted:

```lean
term ::= ...
    | { ident // term }
```

`{ x // p }` is a notation for `[Subtype]](#manual-Subtype___mk) fun (x : _) => p`.

Due to [proof irrelevance]](#manual---tech-term-proof-irrelevance) and [η-equality]](#manual---tech-term-___-equivalence), two elements of a subtype are definitionally equal when the elements of the base type are definitionally equal.
In a proof, the `[ext]](#manual-ext)` tactic can be used to transform a goal of equality of elements of a subtype into equality of their values.

**Example: Definitional Equality of Subtypes**

The non-empty strings `[s1]](#manual-s1-_LPAR_in-Definitional-Equality-of-Subtypes_RPAR_)` and `[s2]](#manual-s2-_LPAR_in-Definitional-Equality-of-Subtypes_RPAR_)` are definitionally equal despite the fact that their embedded proof terms are different.
No case splitting is needed in order to prove that they are equal.

```lean
def NonEmptyString := { x : [String]](#manual-String___ofByteArray) // x ≠ "" }
def s1 : [NonEmptyString]](#manual-NonEmptyString-_LPAR_in-Definitional-Equality-of-Subtypes_RPAR_) :=
⟨"equal", ne_of_beq_false [rfl]](#manual-rfl-next)⟩
def s2 : [NonEmptyString]](#manual-NonEmptyString-_LPAR_in-Definitional-Equality-of-Subtypes_RPAR_) where
[val]](#manual-Subtype___mk) := "equal"
[property]](#manual-Subtype___mk) :=
fun h =>
List.cons_ne_nil _ _ (String.ext_iff.[mp]](#manual-Iff___intro) h)
theorem s1_eq_s2 : [s1]](#manual-s1-_LPAR_in-Definitional-Equality-of-Subtypes_RPAR_) = [s2]](#manual-s2-_LPAR_in-Definitional-Equality-of-Subtypes_RPAR_) := by⊢ [s1]](#manual-s1-_LPAR_in-Definitional-Equality-of-Subtypes_RPAR_) [=]](#manual-Eq___refl) [s2]](#manual-s2-_LPAR_in-Definitional-Equality-of-Subtypes_RPAR_) [rfl]](#manual-rfl)All goals completed! 🐙
```

**Example: Extensional Equality of Subtypes**

The non-empty strings `[s1]](#manual-s1-_LPAR_in-Extensional-Equality-of-Subtypes_RPAR_)` and `[s2]](#manual-s2-_LPAR_in-Extensional-Equality-of-Subtypes_RPAR_)` are definitionally equal.
Ignoring that fact, the equality of the embedded strings can be used to prove that they are equal.
The `[ext]](#manual-ext)` tactic transforms a goal that consists of equality of non-empty strings into a goal that consists of equality of the strings.

```lean
abbrev NonEmptyString := { x : [String]](#manual-String___ofByteArray) // x ≠ "" }
def s1 : [NonEmptyString]](#manual-NonEmptyString-_LPAR_in-Extensional-Equality-of-Subtypes_RPAR_) :=
⟨"equal", ne_of_beq_false [rfl]](#manual-rfl-next)⟩
def s2 : [NonEmptyString]](#manual-NonEmptyString-_LPAR_in-Extensional-Equality-of-Subtypes_RPAR_) where
[val]](#manual-Subtype___mk) := "equal"
[property]](#manual-Subtype___mk) :=
fun h =>
List.cons_ne_nil _ _ (String.ext_iff.[mp]](#manual-Iff___intro) h)
theorem s1_eq_s2 : [s1]](#manual-s1-_LPAR_in-Extensional-Equality-of-Subtypes_RPAR_) = [s2]](#manual-s2-_LPAR_in-Extensional-Equality-of-Subtypes_RPAR_) := by⊢ [s1]](#manual-s1-_LPAR_in-Extensional-Equality-of-Subtypes_RPAR_) [=]](#manual-Eq___refl) [s2]](#manual-s2-_LPAR_in-Extensional-Equality-of-Subtypes_RPAR_)
[ext]](#manual-ext)i✝:[Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero)a✝:[Char]](#manual-Char___mk)⊢ [s1]](#manual-s1-_LPAR_in-Extensional-Equality-of-Subtypes_RPAR_).[val]](#manual-Subtype___mk).toList[[]](#manual-GetElem______mk)i✝[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#GetElem______mk)[?]](#manual-GetElem______mk) [=]](#manual-Eq___refl) [some]](#manual-Option___none) a✝ [↔]](#manual-Iff___intro) [s2]](#manual-s2-_LPAR_in-Extensional-Equality-of-Subtypes_RPAR_).[val]](#manual-Subtype___mk).toList[[]](#manual-GetElem______mk)i✝[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#GetElem______mk)[?]](#manual-GetElem______mk) [=]](#manual-Eq___refl) [some]](#manual-Option___none) a✝
[dsimp]](#manual-dsimp) [only]](#manual-dsimp) [[s1]](#manual-s1-_LPAR_in-Extensional-Equality-of-Subtypes_RPAR_), [s2]](#manual-s2-_LPAR_in-Extensional-Equality-of-Subtypes_RPAR_)]i✝:[Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero)a✝:[Char]](#manual-Char___mk)⊢ "equal".toList[[]](#manual-GetElem______mk)i✝[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#GetElem______mk)[?]](#manual-GetElem______mk) [=]](#manual-Eq___refl) [some]](#manual-Option___none) a✝ [↔]](#manual-Iff___intro) "equal".toList[[]](#manual-GetElem______mk)i✝[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#GetElem______mk)[?]](#manual-GetElem______mk) [=]](#manual-Eq___refl) [some]](#manual-Option___none) a✝
[rfl]](#manual-rfl)All goals completed! 🐙
```

There is a coercion from a subtype to its base type.
This allows subtypes to be used in positions where the base type is expected, essentially erasing the proof that the value satisfies the predicate.

**Example: Subtype Coercions**

Elements of subtypes can be coerced to their base type.
Here, `[nine]](#manual-nine-_LPAR_in-Subtype-Coercions_RPAR_)` is coerced from a subtype of `Nat` that contains multiples of `3` to `[Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero)`.

```lean
abbrev DivBy3 := { x : [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero) // x % 3 = 0 }
def nine : [DivBy3]](#manual-DivBy3-_LPAR_in-Subtype-Coercions_RPAR_) := ⟨9, by⊢ 9 [%]](#manual-HMod___mk) 3 [=]](#manual-Eq___refl) 0 [rfl]](#manual-rfl)All goals completed! 🐙⟩
set_option [eval.type]](#manual-eval___type) true [in]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___in)
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [Nat.succ]](#manual-Nat___zero) [nine]](#manual-nine-_LPAR_in-Subtype-Coercions_RPAR_)
```

```lean
10 : [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero)
```

## Basic Types — 20.21. Lazy Computations {#manual-basic-types-2021-lazy-computations}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Lazy-Computations/

A *thunk* delays the computation of a value.
In particular, the `[Thunk]](#manual-Thunk___mk)` type is used to delay the computation of a value in compiled code until it is explicitly requested—this request is called *forcing* the thunk.
The computed value is saved, so subsequent requests do not result in recomputation.
Computing values at most once, when explicitly requested, is called *lazy evaluation*.
This caching is invisible to Lean's logic, in which `[Thunk]](#manual-Thunk___mk)` is equivalent to a function from `[Unit]](#manual-Unit)`.

### 20.21.1. Logical Model {#manual-Thunk-model}

Thunks are modeled as a single-field structure that contains a function from `[Unit]](#manual-Unit)`.
The structure's field is private, so the function itself cannot be directly accessed.
Instead, `[Thunk.get]](#manual-Thunk___get)` should be used.
From the perspective of the logic, they are equivalent; `[Thunk.get]](#manual-Thunk___get)` exists to be overridden in the compiler by the platform primitive that implements lazy evaluation.

structure

```lean
[Thunk.{u}]](#manual-Thunk___mk) (α : Type u) : Type u



[Thunk.{u}]](#manual-Thunk___mk) (α : Type u) : Type u
```

Delays evaluation. The delayed code is evaluated at most once.

A thunk is code that constructs a value when it is requested via `[Thunk.get]](#manual-Thunk___get)`, `[Thunk.map]](#manual-Thunk___map)`, or
`[Thunk.bind]](#manual-Thunk___bind)`. The resulting value is cached, so the code is executed at most once. This is also
known as lazy or call-by-need evaluation.

The Lean runtime has special support for the `[Thunk]](#manual-Thunk___mk)` type in order to implement the caching
behavior.

Constructor

```lean
[Thunk.mk]](#manual-Thunk___mk).{u}
```

Constructs a new thunk from a function `[Unit]](#manual-Unit) → α` that will be called when the thunk is first
forced.

The result is cached. It is re-used when the thunk is forced again.

Fields

```lean
fn : [Unit]](#manual-Unit) → α
```

Extract the getter function out of a thunk. Use `[Thunk.get]](#manual-Thunk___get)` instead.

### 20.21.2. Runtime Representation {#manual-Thunk-runtime}

m\_header






Lean object header




















m\_value






Saved valuelean\_object \*




















m\_closure






Closurelean\_object \*

Memory layout of thunks

Thunks are one of the primitive object types supported by the Lean runtime.
The object header contains a specific tag that indicates that an object is a thunk.

Thunks have two fields:

- `m_value` is a pointer to a saved value, which is a null pointer if the value has not yet been computed.
- `m_closure` is a closure which is to be called when the value should be computed.

The runtime system maintains the invariant that either the closure or the saved value is a null pointer.
If both are null pointers, then the thunk is being forced on another thread.

When a thunk is [forced]](#manual---tech-term-forcing), the runtime system first checks whether the saved value has already been computed, returning it if so.
Otherwise, it attempts to acquire a lock on the closure by atomically swapping it with a null pointer.
If the lock is acquired, it is invoked to compute the value; the computed value is stored in the saved value field and the reference to the closure is dropped.
If not, then another thread is already computing the value; the system waits until it is computed.

### 20.21.3. Coercions {#manual-Thunk-coercions}

There is a coercion from any type `α` to `[Thunk]](#manual-Thunk___mk) α` that converts a term `e` into `[Thunk.mk]](#manual-Thunk___mk) fun () => e`.
Because the elaborator [unfolds coercions]](#manual-coercion-insertion), evaluation of the original term `e` is delayed; the coercion is not equivalent to `[Thunk.pure]](#manual-Thunk___pure)`.

**Example: Lazy Lists**

Lazy lists are lists that may contain thunks.
The `[delayed]](#manual-LazyList___delayed-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_)` constructor causes part of the list to be computed on demand.

```lean
inductive LazyList (α : Type u) where
| nil
| cons : α → [LazyList]](#manual-LazyList-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_) α → [LazyList]](#manual-LazyList-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_) α
| delayed : [Thunk]](#manual-Thunk___mk) ([LazyList]](#manual-LazyList-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_) α) → [LazyList]](#manual-LazyList-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_) α
[deriving]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___optDeriving-next) [Inhabited]](#manual-Inhabited___mk)
```

Lazy lists can be converted to ordinary lists by forcing all the embedded thunks.

```lean
def LazyList.toList : [LazyList]](#manual-LazyList-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_) α → [List]](#manual-List___nil) α
| [.nil]](#manual-LazyList___nil-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_) => []
| [.cons]](#manual-LazyList___cons-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_) x xs => x :: xs.[toList]](#manual-LazyList___toList-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_)
| [.delayed]](#manual-LazyList___delayed-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_) xs => xs.[get]](#manual-Thunk___get).[toList]](#manual-LazyList___toList-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_)
```

Many operations on lazy lists can be implemented without forcing the embedded thunks, instead building up further thunks.
The body of `[delayed]](#manual-LazyList___delayed-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_)` does not need to be an explicit call to `[Thunk.mk]](#manual-Thunk___mk)` because of the coercion.

```lean
def LazyList.take : [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero) → [LazyList]](#manual-LazyList-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_) α → [LazyList]](#manual-LazyList-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_) α
| 0, _ => .nil
| _, [.nil]](#manual-LazyList___nil-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_) => .nil
| n + 1, [.cons]](#manual-LazyList___cons-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_) x xs => [.cons]](#manual-LazyList___cons-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_) x <| [.delayed]](#manual-LazyList___delayed-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_) <| [take]](#manual-LazyList___take-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_) n xs
| n + 1, [.delayed]](#manual-LazyList___delayed-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_) xs => [.delayed]](#manual-LazyList___delayed-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_) <| [take]](#manual-LazyList___take-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_) (n + 1) xs.[get]](#manual-Thunk___get)
def LazyList.ofFn (f : [Fin]](#manual-Fin___mk) n → α) : [LazyList]](#manual-LazyList-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_) α :=
[Fin.foldr]](#manual-Fin___foldr) n (init := [.nil]](#manual-LazyList___nil-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_)) fun i xs =>
[.delayed]](#manual-LazyList___delayed-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_) <| [LazyList.cons]](#manual-LazyList___cons-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_) (f i) xs
def LazyList.append (xs ys : [LazyList]](#manual-LazyList-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_) α) : [LazyList]](#manual-LazyList-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_) α :=
[.delayed]](#manual-LazyList___delayed-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_) <|
[match]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match) xs [with]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [.nil]](#manual-LazyList___nil-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_) => ys
| [.cons]](#manual-LazyList___cons-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_) x xs' => [LazyList.cons]](#manual-LazyList___cons-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_) x ([append]](#manual-LazyList___append-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_) xs' ys)
| [.delayed]](#manual-LazyList___delayed-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_) xs' => [append]](#manual-LazyList___append-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_) xs'.[get]](#manual-Thunk___get) ys
```

Laziness is ordinarily invisible to Lean programs: there is no way to check whether a thunk has been forced.
However, `dbg_trace` can be used to gain insight into thunk evaluation.

```lean
def observe (tag : [String]](#manual-String___ofByteArray)) (i : [Fin]](#manual-Fin___mk) n) : [Nat]](#manual-Nat___zero) :=
dbg_trace "{tag}: {i.[val]](#manual-Fin___mk)}"
i.[val]](#manual-Fin___mk)
```

The lazy lists `[xs]](#manual-xs-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_)` and `[ys]](#manual-ys-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_)` emit traces when evaluated.

```lean
def xs := [LazyList.ofFn]](#manual-LazyList___ofFn-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_) (n := 3) ([observe]](#manual-observe-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_) "xs")
def ys := [LazyList.ofFn]](#manual-LazyList___ofFn-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_) (n := 3) ([observe]](#manual-observe-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_) "ys")
```

Converting `[xs]](#manual-xs-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_)` to an ordinary list forces all of the embedded thunks:

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [xs]](#manual-xs-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_).[toList]](#manual-LazyList___toList-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_)
```

```lean
xs: 0
xs: 1
xs: 2
```

```lean
[[]](#manual-List___nil)0[,]](#manual-List___nil) 1[,]](#manual-List___nil) 2[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)
```

Likewise, converting `[xs]](#manual-xs-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_).[append]](#manual-LazyList___append-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_) [ys]](#manual-ys-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_)` to an ordinary list forces the embedded thunks:

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [xs]](#manual-xs-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_).[append]](#manual-LazyList___append-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_) [ys]](#manual-ys-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_) |>.[toList]](#manual-LazyList___toList-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_)
```

```lean
xs: 0
xs: 1
xs: 2
ys: 0
ys: 1
ys: 2
```

```lean
[[]](#manual-List___nil)0[,]](#manual-List___nil) 1[,]](#manual-List___nil) 2[,]](#manual-List___nil) 0[,]](#manual-List___nil) 1[,]](#manual-List___nil) 2[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)
```

Appending `[xs]](#manual-xs-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_)` to itself before forcing the thunks results in a single set of traces, because each thunk's code is evaluated just once:

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [xs]](#manual-xs-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_).[append]](#manual-LazyList___append-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_) [xs]](#manual-xs-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_) |>.[toList]](#manual-LazyList___toList-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_)
```

```lean
xs: 0
xs: 1
xs: 2
```

```lean
[[]](#manual-List___nil)0[,]](#manual-List___nil) 1[,]](#manual-List___nil) 2[,]](#manual-List___nil) 0[,]](#manual-List___nil) 1[,]](#manual-List___nil) 2[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)
```

Finally, taking a prefix of `[xs]](#manual-xs-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_).[append]](#manual-LazyList___append-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_) [ys]](#manual-ys-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_)` results in only some of the thunks in `[ys]](#manual-ys-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_)` being evaluated:

```lean
[#eval]](#manual-Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [xs]](#manual-xs-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_).[append]](#manual-LazyList___append-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_) [ys]](#manual-ys-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_) |>.[take]](#manual-LazyList___take-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_) 4 |>.[toList]](#manual-LazyList___toList-_LPAR_in-Lazy-Lists_RPAR_)
```

```lean
xs: 0
xs: 1
xs: 2
ys: 0
```

```lean
[[]](#manual-List___nil)0[,]](#manual-List___nil) 1[,]](#manual-List___nil) 2[,]](#manual-List___nil) 0[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)
```

### 20.21.4. API Reference {#manual-Thunk-api}

def

```lean
[Thunk.get.{u_1}]](#manual-Thunk___get) {α : Type u_1} (x : [Thunk]](#manual-Thunk___mk) α) : α



[Thunk.get.{u_1}]](#manual-Thunk___get) {α : Type u_1}
  (x : [Thunk]](#manual-Thunk___mk) α) : α
```

Gets the thunk's value. If the value is cached, it is returned in constant time; if not, it is
computed.

Computed values are cached, so the value is not recomputed.

def

```lean
[Thunk.map.{u_1, u_2}]](#manual-Thunk___map) {α : Type u_1} {β : Type u_2} (f : α → β)
  (x : [Thunk]](#manual-Thunk___mk) α) : [Thunk]](#manual-Thunk___mk) β



[Thunk.map.{u_1, u_2}]](#manual-Thunk___map) {α : Type u_1}
  {β : Type u_2} (f : α → β)
  (x : [Thunk]](#manual-Thunk___mk) α) : [Thunk]](#manual-Thunk___mk) β
```

Constructs a new thunk that forces `x` and then applies `x` to the result. Upon forcing, the result
of `f` is cached and the reference to the thunk `x` is dropped.

def

```lean
[Thunk.pure.{u_1}]](#manual-Thunk___pure) {α : Type u_1} (a : α) : [Thunk]](#manual-Thunk___mk) α



[Thunk.pure.{u_1}]](#manual-Thunk___pure) {α : Type u_1} (a : α) :
  [Thunk]](#manual-Thunk___mk) α
```

Stores an already-computed value in a thunk.

Because the value has already been computed, there is no laziness.

def

```lean
[Thunk.bind.{u_1, u_2}]](#manual-Thunk___bind) {α : Type u_1} {β : Type u_2} (x : [Thunk]](#manual-Thunk___mk) α)
  (f : α → [Thunk]](#manual-Thunk___mk) β) : [Thunk]](#manual-Thunk___mk) β



[Thunk.bind.{u_1, u_2}]](#manual-Thunk___bind) {α : Type u_1}
  {β : Type u_2} (x : [Thunk]](#manual-Thunk___mk) α)
  (f : α → [Thunk]](#manual-Thunk___mk) β) : [Thunk]](#manual-Thunk___mk) β
```

Constructs a new thunk that applies `f` to the result of `x` when forced.
